JACK R. LEVITT
The talent and leadership qualities of our Grand Master were most evident
to the Craft at large at the 1987 Annual Communication of our Grand Lodge
where he was faced with a huge volume of legislative and other Masonic business. Due in large measure to the administrative abilities of our Grand Master,
this large workload was handled most expeditiously and without the necessity
of holding evening sessions. The entire Communication was conducted with
peace and harmony prevailing. Masonic historians will certainly classify Jack R.
Levitt as one of our most dedicated, devoted and hard-working Grand Masters.
Jack Robert Levitt was born and raised in Los Angeles, California. After
his graduation at Washington High School he attended George Pepperdine
College where he received his B.A. Degree in 1949. He then attended law school
at the U niversity of Southern California where he served as Associate Editor of
the U .S.C. Law Review. He graduated 10th in his class in 1952 with a Bachelor's
Degree in Law. Jack worked his way through college as a movie projectionist
in the Los Angeles area.
After being admitted to the California Bar in 1953 he entered into private
law practice and then accepted an appointment in 1954 as a Deputy District Attorney in San Diego County where he served until December 1956. He then
served briefly as Assistant City Attorney in La Mesa and re-entered private law
practice from 1957 until 1972, handling primarily plaintifPs personal injury
work.
In March 1972, then Governor Ronald Reagan appointed him to the Superior Court Bench in the County of San Diego. He was subsequently elected
and re-elected as a Judge of this Court and continues to serve thereon at this
time. Judge Levitt is very active in the legal community in California, serving
with great distinction as a lecturer, panelist, author and instructor in a great
many subjects in the practice of civil and criminal law as well as procedures and
administrative matters in the court system. He holds membership in various
professional and community organizations. He is one of the two judges who
were instrumental in implementing the "FAST TRACK" plan in the San Diego
County Superior Courts. This is a system of expediting the processing of cases
through the court system, thus greatly improving the administration of justice.
While attending Pepperdine College, Jack met and fell in love with the lovely Kay Daubenberger. They were married in 1954 and were blessed with three
lovely children. Their daughter Kristy is an Elementary School teacher in Montana while daughter Pam is touring and sight-seeing around the country. Their
son Steve is a Professor at the University of Kentucky.

JACK R. LEVITT
Grand Master
October 15, 1986 - October 15, 1987

Kay has truly been the "First Lady of Masonry" in our Jurisdiction during
this Masonic year because she has not only been a great pillar of support for
Ill

our Grand Master, but she has also won the hearts of our members with her
warm and friendly smile and her pleasant and winning personality. Since her
alma mater is U.C.L.A. she and Jack can engage in some friendly rivalry
whenever U.C.LA. and U.S.C. are engaged 10 athletic contests.
Our Grand Master was raised to the Sublime Degree of Master Mason in
Silver Trowel Lodge No. 415 on April 22, 1953. In 1960 he transferred his membership to San Diego Lodge No. 35 where he served as Master in 1979. He is a
. Charter Member of Joseph L. Shell Daylight Lodge No. 837. He holds membership in the York Rite Bodies and served for two years as Venerable Master
of the San Diego Bodies of the Scottish Rite. He was Coroneted a 33rd Degree
Inspector General (Honorary) in 1971 and is currently the Chairman of the
Sovereign Grand Inspector General's Advisory Conference in San Diego and
Vice-President of the California Scottish Rite Foundation. He is a member of
the cast in several of the Scottish Rite degrees and serves as Classroom Lecturer.
Brother Levitt is a member of Al Bahr Temple, AAONMS where he serves on the Ritual Divan, often taking the part of Potentate. He is Past Sovereign
of the Red Cross of Constantine and still plays a major rqle in the conferral of
the Orders therein. Other Masonic affiliations include Royal Order of Jesters,
Quetta Grotto, Hi-Twelve, DeMolay Preceptory (is Honorary DeMolay Legion
of Honor), National Sojourners and Heroes of '76 (Honorary) and Southern
California Research Lodge.

His Grand Lodge activities include service on the Lodge Resources and
Development Committee, Laymen's Night Speakers Panel, Masters and Wardens Workshop and Jurisprudence Comrniltcc, serving as the latter's Chairman
for several years. He served our Grand Lodge as its Senior Grand Deacon in

Because of his speaking abilities and his deep understanding and
knowledge of Masonic philosophy and teachings, he was and is in great demand
as a speaker on Masonic subjects. His expertise in conducting cornerstone
ceremonies entirely from memory has become legendary (20 ceremonies during
his year as Grand Master). Despite the many problems which required his personal attention as Grand Master, Jack administered all matters with firmness
and fairness, always keeping uppermost in his mind his duty to uphold our Constitution and Ordinances.
The theme of Most Worshipful Brother Levitt's year as Grand Master was
to "Accentuate the Positive". This was emphasized in all of his talks and
ceremonies as he traveled extensively throughout the Jurisdiction. Many of our
Brethren received and wore one of the "positive" buttons in support of his theme.
Our Grand Master also took great delight in reciting poetry to put across a point.
The Fraternity can be thankful that he will be in our midst for many years to
come to lend his assitance to Freemasonry.

ONE HUNDRED IBIRTY-EIGHTH
ANNUAL COMMUNICATION
The One Hundred Thirty-Eighth Annual Communication of the Most
Worshipful Grand Lodge, Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California commenced at 9:00 A.M. on Monday, October 12, 1987, AL. 5987 in the
California Masonic Memorial Temple located in San Francisco, California.
Prior to the opening of Grand Lodge, an organ recital was presented by
Grand Organist Harold M. Hand.
The opening session of the Annual Communication was raised by Gerald
Winstanley the Master of San Diego Lodge No. 35, the Lodge of Grand Master
Jack R. Levitt, and Chester Rogers a Past Master of the same Lodge. The gavel
used to raise the opening session had been hand crafted by Chester Rogers and
was presented to the Grand Master at a reception given in his honor by San
Diego Lodge No. 35 on April 25, 1987. Other gavels which were used by the
Grand Master during the Monday morning session were as follows: a gavel
made of eucalyptus wood, crafted by Darrel McCormick, a member of Woodland Lodge No. 81 and presented to the Grand Master at a reception for him
by the 210th Masonic District held on June 26, 1987 and a gavel made of California desert ironwood and Kiaue wood from Hawaii crafted by Glenn Johnson a
Past Master and Secretary of San Dimas Lodge No. 428 which was presented
to the Grand Master at reception given him by the 610th Masonic District on
November 14, 1986.
Responding to the call of the roll were the following Grand Lodge Officers,
elected and appointed, the Past Grand Masters and Past Grand Officers:

The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California was opened
in ample form, with the Grand Master presiding. The Flag of our Country was
formally received and presented at the Altar, after which the assembled
Brethren joined in the Pledge of Allegiance to the Flag.
Present during the Communication were 1062 officers and representatives
from 526 chartered Lodges and 1 U.D. Lodge, 1075 Past Masters, 365 Master
Masons not members of Grand Lodge, and 37 Distinguished Guests from other
Grand Jurisdictions. Twenty-nine Grand Lodge 0 fticers of this Jurisdiction as
well as 19 Past Grand Masters and 2 Past Grand Officers were registered. The
total attendance count was 2589.

to serve on the Committee were Verne W. Hendrix, Past Grand Secretary, and

"What can be more palpably absurd than the prospect held out of locomotives traveling twice as fast as stage coaches. Why every intelligent person knows
that at 40 miles per hour a human being would die from the speed!" National
Quarterly Review (1825)
At the tum of the century the head of the U.S. Patent Office went so far as
to declare that "Just about everything that is going to be invented has already
been invented."
The noted writer H.G. Wells could envision Martians coming to earth, but
he couldn't accept the invention of the submarine. He rejected the whole idea
as being absurd. He insisted that everyone in the boat would suffocate and the
boat would flounder at sea.
Not long ago Reader's Digest gave a list of excuses which have been offered
in court by otherwise seemingly intelligent people:
"A pedestrian hit me and went under my car."
•coming home I drove into the wrong house and collided with a tree I don't
have."
"The pedestrian had no idea which direction to run, so I ran over him."
"The indirect cause of the accident was a little guy in a small car with a big
mouth."
I tried to save the best for the last. "I pulled away from the side of the road,
glanced at my mother-in-law and headed over the embankment."
Absurd as these may sound to us, they are no more absurd than some of
the suggestions I have heard to increase our membership and improve our f mancial position.
From our "Great Light" (1 Samuel 17:45) comes an ancient story which
many learned as children, but it bears repeating for its lessons while very old,
are ever new. In this Biblical story we hear of a group of Israelites who said, "It
can't be done." There was also a young man named David who said, "It could
be done." A group of the enemy called "Philistines" gathered on the ridge of a
hill near the city of Bethelehem. A valley and a small stream separated the opposing forces. The Philistines sent forth their champion, one named Goliath of
Gath. He was a giant to end all giants. His height was six cubits (about 91/2 feet):
he weighed somewhere in the area of 600 lbs. He was covered with brass with a
helmet of brass. He wore a coat of mail and a shield carrier was set before him.
The tip of his sword weighed 20 lbs. H e filled the Israelies with terror. King Saul
offered many inducements to any one who would accept the challenge. No one
would accept the chaJlenge even when the King offered great wealth and even
his own daughter in marriage. These rewards were disdained by the young
David. He declared that his only interest was to show the whole world that there

raphy, history or our national purpose? Perhaps even worse, college class rooms
where these ideas are derided and sneered at. I believe that this is a challenge

A college football coach was faced with the possibility that his star player
might be declared academically ineligible, so he pleaded with the mathematics
professor not to flunk the kid. "Tell you what, coach," said the professor, "I'll
pass him." The athlete was called in, and the professor asked, "What's two and
two?" "Four" replied the player. Frantically the coach cried, "Give him another
chance, give him another chance." Is this our idea of a good education either
Masonic or public?

NECROLOGY REPORT
Most Worshipful (;rand Master and the Brethren of lhe Grand Lodge:
The members of the Memorial Service Committee are very grateful to have
this opportunity to serve the Brethren of this Grand Lodge, and lead in a final
tribute for our deceased Brethren.
It is fitting then, my Brethren, as we commence this our one hundred and
thirty-eighth Annual Communica tion to pause and pay homage to those
Brethren of this jurisdiction, who in this last year, have gone before us.
In the ritual of our Craft, we utilize many working tools and emblems. They
remind us of Life, Death, and Hope of Immortality. We are told "that we are
traveling upon that level of time to that undiscovered country from whose bourn
no traveler returns."
That we should live a clean and uprighteo us life, and that we should practice those Masonic principals of Brotherly Love, Relief, and Truth we are also
told.
"But there will come a time and the wisest know not how soon, when all distinction, save that of goodness will cease, and Death, the mighty leveler of
human greatness, reduce us to the same state."
Death then is a separation. ll alludes to sepa.rations of all kinds. No t only
is there a physical phenomenon , where the whole human body ceases to function, but it also means a separation from the most obvious aspects of living.

Separation from loved ones and valued people. Separation from precious things
and places. Death has power because we are afraid of it. Some believe that if
we don't talk about it, we can keep it down and it is hidden. ls Death then ruling
our lives? The moment we let Death distract us from the fact that God, in His
infinite mercy, is our help in ages past; that our God has created and provided
for all things, then if you believe this distraction, we are doomed.

Death is not the worse thing in life. A few years ago, I had a neighbor, a
brother Master Mason, who al the time was 83 years old. He was a farmer all
his life, but he had a history of heart trouble. He loved nothing more than to be
out in the fresh air, and tilling and working the soil. Planting and pruning fruit
trees, vegetables,watching them grow, and harvesting them at the proper time.
His children and grandchildren were afraid that he was going to have
another heart attack. They would say to him, "Dad, be careful, you know your
heart isn't what it used lo be." He would answer, "I know, but I'd much rather
be out here working when I have my next heart attack, then lying around in bed,
doing nothing, and waiting for it. That's a far better way for me to spend my life,
then just lying around trying lo protect myself." He was right, he was absolutely right. He chose where he wanted to spend his life, and he preferred dying
doing meaningful productive things.
Like my farme~ friend, :-ve put our "Trust in God". But yet, we often forget
that God also put htS Trust m us. He created this world we live in. He created
the heaven, the i:arth, a?d all the creatur7s that dwell within. God expects us
to take care of His creation. We put trust m Him, but he also puts trust in us.
. There ar7 things in life wors~ ~ha~ Death. Having no purpose in life is one
of thel?. HaVlng no reason for liV1ng IS worse than dying. A Mason's view of
Death is really a Mason's view of Life. That is what a Mason's view of Life is all
about. We are given the opportunity to serve mankind, particularly our Brother
Masons, the World, and not to worry about Death.
. Our ri~ual teaches us "that Life is so uncertain, and that all material purSUJts arc ~am, let us no longer postpone the all important concern of preparing
for eterruty, but let 1:15 embrace the present moment, while time and o pportunity
ar~ offer~d, to proVl~e for that great change when all the pomp and pleasure of
this fleet mg world wt!I pall upon the senses, and the recollection of a virtuous
and well-spent life will yield the only comfort and consolation."

In reflect.ing upo n the membership record of this last year, we see that the
destroyer of hfe has affected our Brothers in many walks of life, in a great percentages of our Lodges, and from many different areas of our jurisdiction. The
sha~ow o.f death has again made its appearence and saddened our hearts.
Dunng this last year we ~ave lost 5633 members within our jurisdiction. Of this,
530 were members of this Grand Lodge; two Worshipful Masters, one Senior
Warden, one Junior Warden, and 526 Past Masters. 362 Lodges have recorded

As there are no Memorial Tributes or Eulogies this morning, the Memorial
Service Committee would like to mention two brothers for their labors in the
vineyards of Masonry. They are: W. RichardJ. Pierce, P.M. member of Yount
Lodge No. 12. Chairman of this Committee in 1985, former Grand Bible Bearer,
who served on many committees of this Grand Lodge. W. Bernhardt A. Berliner, P .M. member of Fidelity Lodge, No.120. Chairman of this Committee in
1986 and who served on it for ten years.

To alJ the deceased Brethren, we are thankful for their lives. We will miss
their sincere friendships and their contributions to our great Fraternity. We
know that they are all dwelling in God's Everlasting Kingdom enjoying a just
reward for a virtuous and well-spent life.

Devotional Prayer:
Almighty God, our heavenly Father, we thank Thee this day for aU those of
our beloved Fraternity of Free and Accepted Masons who have gone to be with
Thee since our last Communication. W c thank Thee for thy love that continually surrounds us whether in life or in death. Sanctify to us the beautiful memories
of the past. May we continue faithful in our present trust as members of our
Craft so that as our even tide comes, we too may be called to that Eternal Home
not made with hands which God has prepared for us. Amen.

REPORT OF THE GRAND SECRETARY
REPORT OF THE GRAND TREASURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A . M. of California:
The financial records of Grand Lodge and its several entities have been examined by the accounting firm of Lindquist, Von Husen and Joyce, performing
the required verification of assets and have commented on matters requiring
management attention. The several reports of the auditors for the fiscal year
ending June 30, 1987, have been pre-printed as part of this Grand Treasurer's
report. They are available for your inspection and comment.
All the financial records are maintained in the Grand Lodge office under
the supervision of Hugo Delfin, Manager of Accounting, who reports to and
works very closely with the Grand Treasurer. In his six years plus with Grand
Lodge Mr. Delfin has put in place a dedicated an<l professional group of
employees who well understand their collective responsibilities in respect to the
accounting methods of Grand Lodge. The accounting department serves you,
the Grand Lodge membership, in a sound, business-like way, and their methods
and procedures should never be altered simply to satisfy individual desires.
The office of the Grand Treasurer has always observed carefully the fiscal
matters of Grand Lodge. You, as members of Grand Lodge, are urged to be
aware of the financial condition of Grand Lodge and to review the report of the
Finance Committee.
You have permitted me to serve this great Masonic family for more than
twenty years and I am deeply indebted for the opportunity to enjoy so many fine
Masonic friends.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A . M. of California:
My Brethren:
Once again I am pleased to present to the members of this Grand Lodge
the report of the Grand Secretary, covering the transactions and business for
the fiscal year ending on June 30, 1987.
Section 1108-4th mandates that all monies collected which are due the
Grand Lodge be paid to the Grand Treasurer. This has been done and these
monies have been credited to the proper accounts as reflected in the Grand
Treasurer's printed report audited by our Certified Public Accountants. All
supporting books, vouchers and receipts are maintained and are on file in the
accounting department of the Grand Lodge office.
Also maintained and on file are all of the minutes of those meetings held
by the various Boards of Trustees -- Masonic Homes, Memorial Temple and
Masonic Foundation, as well as meetings of the Investment, Retirement and Executive Committees of the Grand Lodge. The Finance Committee met with the
Executive Committee and others who arc involved with the preparation of the
operating budget of the Grand Lodge for the year 1987-1988 and their report
and recommendations will be presented to you during the course of this Annual
Communication. At my suggestion the Finance Committee, this year, has estimated the additional amount of per capita which will be required should certain Resolutions submitted for consideration, be approved and these estimated
additional amounts have been printed at the bottom of those Resolutions.
I would be rei;niss if I did not once again express my admiration to those
members of our various Boards and Committees of this Grand Lodge with
whom our office comes into frequent contact. It is a genuine pleasure to work
with these dedicated Masons

Thank you and goodbye. God bless you all.

UNFINISHED BUSINESS
Respectfully submitted,

JOHN A. SICKENDERGER, Grand Treasurer

The Grand Lodge computer system which was proposed and approved by
the delegates at the 1985 Annual Communication, has been completed and
placed into service in the Membership section of your Grand Lodge office.
Our new system is comprised of AT&T equipment, more specifically(!)
3Bl computer with a 67 megabyte internal hard disk and 3.5 megabytes of Random Access Memory and (1) 610 Terminal.
The operating system is AT&T Unix System V, version 3.5. In addition, we
have installed the Starlan network software. This enables all three stations to
access both hard disks, thereby providing as close to a MultiUser environment
as possible which was the original intent when this system was approved. The
network software was necessitated due to the extra large number of records in
our data base, the Data Base program and the limitations which AT&T
designed into the structure of both computers.
With this project completed, we would like to advise the Craft that with our
awareness of ever increasing costs, the Grand Lodge Computer System was
developed, purchased and installed for an amount well below that which was
budgeted and approved at the 1985 and 1986 Annual Communication. In addition, cost savings will result with respect to a great deal of printing which our
office does and also in costs charged to the California Freemason Magazine.
Much of the effort devoted to the development and installation of our computer
system was expended by Brother Kenn eth J. Brisbin, Chairman of our Membership Department and my personal appreciation is extended to him for the
many hours he devoted to this task. These hours included nights as well as weekends.

GRAND LODGE OFFICE PERSONNEL
During this past year several of our long-time office employees retired. It
is not always easy to find personnel to replace those who, because of their years
of service, have performed their various job functions in a most efficient manner. However, I'm most pleased to report that we have been extremely fortunate
in securing the services of people who have assumed their respective assignments and have shown the willingness and ability to learn our office procedures.
All are performing in a most creditable manner. I would particularly like to
mention Brother Michael Price, a Past Master of Paul Revere Lodge No. 462,
who assumed the supervision of our Supply and Mail Room upon the retirement of Marian Thomas after thirty years of service. This is a key position in
our office and Brother Price has shown that he is well qualified to supervise the
many duties and responsibilities in connection with this important post.
My sincere thanks is extended to all our office personnel, old and new alike.

It is a pleasure to work with these people who insure that our office procedures
remain effective and as efficient as we can make them.

32

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

HAWAII MEETINGS
In 1984 I journeyed to Hawaii to meet with those interested members of

each of the Lodges located in the islands. Three years having elapsed since
those meetings, and with the concurrence of the members of the Executive Committee, I again visited the Islands in May of this year and held five separate meetings. Those in attendance were most appreciative of receiving the information
I was able to impart to them and conversely I appreciated their interest by being
in attendance.The kindnesses and hospitality accorded to my wife and myself
was truly gratifying and our sincere thanks is extended to those who made our
visitation so enjoyable. My particular appreciation goes to Assistant Grand
Lecturer Albert Farias of Division VU who arranged our itinerary and
scheduled the various meetings which were held on four of the islands.Personal
contact between the Grand Lodge office and the Lodges of Hawaii is just as important as the same contact which exists between our office and the Lodges in
California.

SECRETARIES' ASSOCIATIONS
Meetings of Lodge Secretaries organized in associations throughout the
jurisdiction continue to be held on a quarterly basis. These associations have
been formed over the years on a voluntary basis and at each meeting, representatives from the Grand Lodge office are in attendance to review the
mechanics of the law as it relates to the duties and responsibilities of the Lodge
Secretary. These informal meetings provide an excellent forum for an exchange
of ideas which, I believe, is beneficial both to the Lodge Secretary and to the
Grand Lodge office. As an example of this, our Assistant Grand Secretary
recently prevailed upon the Chairman of the Grand Lodge Insurance Committee to have a member of that committee attend each association meeting and
address those in attendance on matters of insurance as they pertain to Lodges
and Temple Associations. All benefited greatly from these presentations. It is
anticipated that for future meetings, other committee members wiJl be asked to
speak on matters pertaining to their respective committees.We would hope that
all Lodge Secretaries would make it a point to attend these meetings and encourage the officers of their respective Lodges and any interested member to
accompany them. We also welcome the attendance of District Inspectors. Not
only are these meetings informative, but good Masonic fellowship always
prevails.

APPRECIATl ON
In concluding this annual report, I must express my appreciation to all who
labor for the benefit and advancement of our Fraternity. As in all of our sister
jurisdictions, we are faced with serious problems - some external, many internal. However, if we persevere and "accentuate the positive" a good many of
these problems will be overcome and we can look forward to a bright future. I
must express my gratitude to Grand Master Jack R. Levitt and the members of

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

33

the Executive Committee who have expended untold hours of effort in addressing the many problems with which we are beset. Their manner of handling these
problems is both thoughtful and professional and amply demonstrates those
leadership qualities for which they have been elected. I also must express my
gratitude and appreciation to those members of our several Committees and
Boards as well as our Inspectors with whom our office works in close co-operation. Masonry is truly a co-operative effort. For the privilege of serving in my
present capacity, I sincerely thank the members of this Grand Lodge. It is a
most gratifying experience.
Respectfully submitted,

G and Secretary

ACTION BY GRAND LODGE
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence has reviewed 267 approved Applicationsfor Dispensation, and finds that Grand Master Levitt acted properly within
his executive powers and Masonic law in each instance.

As with the Resolutions to be voted upon, this has been a banner year for
Dispensations with roughly twice the average number having been submitted by
the Craft Lodges. In numerous instances, those not conforming to law or practice were first clarified with Lodge Secretaries or Masters by the Grand
Secretary. Next they were reviewed and approved by the Grand Master. Finally, they were reviewed, and in some instances further clarified, prior to ultimate
approval by the Committee on Jurisprudence. This process has served the Craft

36

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

well in insuring conformity throughout our Jurisdiction of Masonic law, policy
and practice.
Grand Secretary Klinger in his Report has classified the numerous Dispensations by subject matter. Although his numbers differ somewhat from ours due
to the fact that we continue our review after his Report bas been submitted to
the printers, we are certain that it must be tremendously gratifying to the Grand
Master to note the Craft's response to his urging that we be more visible to the
public, for there were approved 134 Applications for Dispensations to participate in a parade or to wear Masonic regalia at public functions.
Applications for Dispensations to hold special elections for Wardens and
Masters who either are not elected or installed within the statutory time, or when
those offices become vacant after Installation continues to be a problem area
and one requiring greater attention by senior Lodge Officers, Lodge
Secretaries, and Inspectors while acting in their Districts as representatives of
the Grand Master. We direct your special attention to Sections 2500, 2502 and
2524 of the California Masonic Code at election and installation time this next
Masonic Year to insure that Applications for Dispensation are timely requested
if Masters or Wardens are not elected, or fail to qualify, or if such offices become vacant.
Your Committee on Jurisprudence also reviews Resolutions to modify the
cost of life memberships (primarily as a result of a change in annual dues) and
Resolutions to rescind plans. The three Resolutions to rescind and the 43 to increase costs were all approved.
Our task is significantly eased by the full cooperation of the Office of the
Grand Secretary, and we are, accordingly, indebted to Very Worshipful Brother
Robert A. Klinger and his staff.
Respectfully submitted,
Donald B. McCaw, C/Jainnan

Donald J. Drew
Allen B. Gresham
Charles W. Foster

TRIAL RECORD NO. 2198
Your Committee has considered a Petition for Restoration in Trial Record
No. 2198 by a former member of Solano Lodge No. 2'1.9 who was expelled by
this Grand Lodge after being found guilty by his Lodge in 1984 of Insurance
Fraud.
A Petition for Restoration was denied by this Grand Lodge at its Annual
Communication in 1985. The former Brother has once again petitioned for restoration which, once again, your Committee recommends be denied.
Membership in our Fraternity is, must, and should be zealously guarded.
Once membership is lost by an act of unmasonic conduct, restoration for the
rights and privileges as well as the duties and obligations should be granted only
after there exists clear and convincing evidence of atonement and rehabilitation.
The former Brother has substantial expression of support from his former
Lodge and other members of his community. Given the gravity of the Charge
your Committee does not feel that sufficient time has elapsed, or rehabilitation
has occurred to insure a complete restoration to the principles of Masonic conduct.
Your Committee therefore submits this following resolution:
RESOLVED, that in Trial Record 2198 the Petition for Restoration be
denied.
Report ADOPTED.
TRIAL RECORD NO. 2200
Your Committee has considered an application for restoration in Trial
Record numbered 2200 by a member of Meridian Lodge No. 105 in the Grand
Lodge of Montana, who was expelled from the rights and privileges of Masons
in California by action of this Grand Lodge in 1984.
We are of the opinion that the former Brother has shown sufficient realization of the circumstances that lead lo his expulsion, and our Committee is satisfaed with his change of outlook, his rehabilitation and acceptance by his
community. Sufficient time has elapsed lo indicate these positive factors are not
merely temporary changes.
Your Committee therefore submits the following Resolution:
RESOLVED that the Application for Restoration in Trial Record numbered 2200 be approved.
Report ADOPTED.

TRIAL RECORD NO. 2256
In Trial Record No. 2256, a member and Past Master of Libertas-Security
Lodge No. 466 was charged with Grand Theft as a result of the theft of irrigation pipe.

As originally filed, the Charges alleged only that the Accused had been tried
and found guilty of the Felony of Grand Theft and that the Accused had been
sentenced therefore.
Upon receipt of the Charges, the Grand Secretary's office informed the
Lodge that the Charges were not specific and suggested that they be amended.
Amended Charges were filed, however the amended charge still stated only that
on a certain date a Trial was held at which the Accused was found guilty of a
Felony. The Chairman of this Committee again informed the Lodge that a conviction by a Court or Jury is not in itself a Masonic offense. What is a Masonic
offense is the commission of the Grand Theft itself. Specific wording of a valid
charge was provided. Libertas-Security Lodge No. 466 chose to ignore the advice and did not amend its Charges.
Therefore no valid charge of any Masonic offense exists upon which the
Accused can prepare a defense. To complicate matters further, the Accused
submitted a letter to the Lodge which contained a denial of his guilt, yet no
Masonic Trial was held and the matter was treated as though no response had
been made by the Accused.
The Trial Master based his finding of guilt upon the Accused's conviction
of Grand Theft in the Criminal Court, and fixed the penalty at Suspension.
Your Committee believes that there exists serious deficiencies in both procedure and due process and therefore submits the following Resolution:
RESOLVED, that the Trial Master's Verdict of Guilty and the penalty of
Suspension be reversed and that this matter be remanded to Libertas-Security
Lodge No. 466 for proceeding in accordance with this opinion.
Report ADOPTED.
TRJAL RECORD NO. 2257

In Trial Record No. 2257, a member of Normal Heights Lodge No. 632 was
charged with unmasonic conduct on the grounds that he knowingly and willingly filed a fraudulent Federal Tax Return for 1984. In his letter lo the Lodge,
responding lo the Charges, the Accused admitted that he had pleaded guilty in
Federal Court to these Charges and attempted to minimize them, but he did
not defend against them. The Trial Master found him guilty and fixed the penalty al Suspension.
Your Committee on Trial Review believes that the acts of the Accused arc
of sufficient severity that the penalty should be raised from Suspension to Expulsion.

We therefore submit the following Resolution:

RESOLVED, that the findings of the Trial Master in Trial Record No. 2257
be affirmed, but the penalty be raised to Expulsion.
Report ADOPTED.
TRIAL RECORD NO. 2264
The accused in Trial Record No. 2264, a member of Sierra Lodge No. 788,
was accused of "Sexual Battery".
To this charge he entered a plea of not guilty. A trial was held and the penalty was assessed as Expulsion.
Your Committee has carefully reviewed the entire file, including a
"transcript" prepared by the Secretary and has found a number of procedural
and other due process errors. Your Committee concludes that these errors
deprived the accused of a fair trial. In part, they arc as follows:

1. The accused was probably in custody when the trial was held.
2. The Trial Master gave the appearance of being the accuser.
3. The record is devoid of any testimony by the accuser.
4. The only evidence upon which the Commission could act was a copy
of the criminal record in which the accused entered a plea of guilty; and,
it appeared that the Trial Master independently determined such to be
J?rima facie evidence of guilt and the Trial Master took the question of
oetermination of guilt away from the Commission.
5. Notwit~stimding the Record of De!ermination shoy.ing that the
Com.mission found the accused guilty, the "transcnpt" reflects that the
Trial Master never requested a vote on the guilt phase but directed the
Commission to determine sentence only.
Under the circumstances, your committee has no alternative but to reverse
and remand for new trial. Your committee further deems it necessary to instruct
the new Commission and the Trial Master to follow procedural and other due
process requirements which, in part, include the taking of evidence of guilt and
a determination by the Commission of the guilt or innocence of the accused
Your committee also recommends the appointment of a different Trial
Master.
Your committee therefore submits the following Reso lution:
RESOLVED, that theJudgment in Trial Record No. 2264 be reversed and
remanded to the Lodge for retrial by a newly appointed Trial Master and newly
elected Commission.
Report NOT ADOPTED

TRIAL RECORD NO. 22£>9
In Trial Record No. 2269, a member of Los Alamitos Lodge No. 809 was
charged with three specifications of unmasonic conduct. Two specifications
arise as a result of being found guilty of unmasonic conduct in Tennessee and
one as a result of alleged unmasonic conduct in California. At the March 1987
Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Tennessee, the member was expelled from the Masonic Fraternity in the State of Tennessee.
Los Alamitos Lodge conducted a Masonic Trial by Commission. The
specifications in general were:

1. He falsely accused a member of Beaver Ridge Lodge No. 366, Knoxville, Tennessee of wronir;fully collecting funds from Knoxville Scottish
Rite Bodies that involvea travel to and from Washington, D.C. on
official Scottish Rite business.
2. He falsely accused a member of Beaver Ridge Lodge No. 366,
Knoxville, Tennessee, of wrongfully transferring title to an automobile
from Knoxville Lodges of Perfection to himself.
3. In a letter dated September 2, 1986, he resigned from California
Masonry and renounced all oaths and obligations. On September 24,
1986, he withdrew the resignation and renunciation. Theo on October 3,
1986, he reaffirmed his act to resign from M asonry.
The Los Alamitos Lodge Trial Commission found the member not guilty
of specifications one and two and guilty of specification three. The Commission
voted to fix the penalty at Reprimand.
Your Trial Review Committee concurs with the findings of the Commission but respcctf~lly disagrees with the penalty.
Section 3306 of the California Masonic Code provides in part:
"The following acts committed by a Mason against his Lodge or the Master
thereof shall constitute unmasoo1c conduct sufficient to support the filing of
charges against such Mason ...
(c)Attemptcd resignation for or renunciation of Masonry...."
A thorough review of the record herein clearly demonstrated that the member was attempting to use his resignation and renunciation of Masonry as a ploy
io prevent the State of Tennessee from exercising its authority under their
Masonic Code.
At the member's Los Alamitos trial, he again vacillated regarding whether
he was or was not still desirous of resigning/renouncing Masonry. Your Trial
Review Committee concludes that the selective use of resignation/renunciation
at the whim of the member when it best serves his personal purposes is offensive and detrimental to Masonry. Based on the foregoing, your committee
believes that these actio ns are of sufficient severity that the Penalty should be
raised from Reprimand to Suspension.

We therefore submit the following Resolution:
RESOLVED, that the findings of the Trial Commission be affirmed, but
the Penalty be raised to Suspension.
Report ADOPTED.

TRIAL RECORD NO. 2272
In Trial Record No. 2272, a member of Tri Square Lodge No. 551 was
charged with urunasonic conduct in that he was convicted on his plea (nolo contendere) of the cultivating of marijuana in violation of Section 11358 of the
California Health and Safety Code, a felony.
The Accused did not respond to the Charges and the Trial Master found
the Accused Guilty and fixed the Penalty at Expulsion.
Your Committee on Trial Review found that the Trial Record as submitted
to Grand Lodge did not contain sufficient specifications to sustain a finding of
unmasonic conduct. Allegations of a conviction in a Criminal Court is not itself
a Masonic offense. Both the Chairman of this Committee and the Grand
Secretary suggested to the Lodge that the Charges be amended to set forth appropriate charges of facts indicating unmasonic conduct and be served on the
Accused. The Accused would then have an opportunity to respond to proper
Charges. We cannot sustain a conviction based upon the present Charges which
do not allege a Masonic offense.
Your Committee therefore offers the following Resolution:
RESOLVED, that the Verdict of Guilty of the Trial Master and the Penalty of Expulsion be reversed and this matter be remanded to Tri Square Lodge
No. 551 for further proceedings in accord with this opinion.
Report ADOPTED.

REPORT OF THE GRAND LECTURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California:
Brethren -- in accordance with Section #1114-4th of o ur ordinances it is
the duty of the G rand Lecturer to make an annual r eport. As I have held this
office for less than four weeks, I can assure you that it will be brief.
RITUAL CONFERENCES
The divisional conferences for Inspectors and Ritual Committee meetings
were held as follows:
DIV: VI - January 16-18, in Ontario, arranged by Worshipful Edwin A.
R obinson.
DIV .. V - February 20-22, in Oxnard, arranged by Worshipful Samuel E.
Harns.

Koula.
DIV I~ - April 10-12, in Sacramento, arranged by Worshipful D onald K.
Baldwm.

.

DIV: I - June 19-21, in Oakland, arranged by Worshipful Edward P. Margheno.
Other ritual meetings were held throughout the year, as were necessary. In
addition, seminars wer e conducted in the Jurisdiction and were well received
and very productive.
COR NERSTONE CEREMONY

UNION CITY OPERATIONS

!. Burton Brown, Administrator
Tbe event that received the most attention this year was centered around
the plans for the expansion projects. In September the city of Union City gave
approval for a secondary access road, but grading and construction was delayed
until April. On March 15 the Grand Master and Grand Lodge Officers conducted Ground Breaking Ceremonies for the Board of Trustees. And in
preparation for the new buildings, the Administrator's house was vacated as it
will soon be demolished.
As this report is published, the road will be completed; grading and demolition of an existing parking lot should be finished; and the foundations for the
new buildings will be under way. Also, within this year's projects was the
demolition of Siminoff Temple, which had stood in place since 1903.
During the year our computerized Energy Management System and
economy obtained by the use of alternate sources of fuel for our utilities,
negotiated rates, and modification of some equipment allowed us to enjoy a
savings of $74,000. In keeping with the times, we have added additional computer equipment and trained some employees to utilize it to expedite record
keeping and procedures in certain areas. As an example, in our Skilled Nursing Facility we retain all Physicians' orders, medication requirements, treatments, diets and nutritional supplements for every resident within a computer
and are easily able to produce accurate up-to-date records whenever needed.
We also have installed a computer in the Administrator's offic.e for word
processing and compiling the necessary statistical records . The
Administrator's Secretary, Helen Morrison (who joined us in October '86 as a
replacement for Kate Huggard, who moved to Washington) possesses the skills
needed to implement the above programs and to improve other aspects of the
administrative office.
We initiated two-way communication with CB radio between our vehicles
used for transporting residents and a base station at the Home. This also
provides more economical use of drivers and vehicles, plus offering more convenience for the residents.
Included in the operations this year was our entry into a contract with an
Environmental Services company to manage our laundry and housekeeping
departments. This also has eroven to afford us some savings, while retaining
our own employees and utilizing their management personnel. In addition, this
arrangement has provided us with more expertise and experienced management personnel.
In an effort to maintain top quality of care for the residents, a new 17 passenger bus was purchased to replace a vehicle acquired in 1976. This bus serves the Home as a multipurp<>se vehicle in that it can transport a combination
of ambulatory, wheel-charr, and/or stretcher type residents. Through a
generous donor, we also acquired a 12 passenger van which eliminated us from
purchasing a replacement for one of our station wagons.

Construction is about to get under way on the new Adult Center which comprises a community building and the first phase of the new adult apartments.

This phase includes two single story buildings each housing 14 apartments and
a two story building of similar design housing 28 apartments, making a total of
56 apartments housing up to 112 ambulatory residents capable of semi-independent living. The apartments are designed for use by couples but the Board
will entertain applicahons from single residents, also. In addition, some minor
modifications are being made to tlie present Children's facilities, a garage is
being remodeled for use as a maintenance building and a security gate and guard
house are being installed at the main entrance. As part of the overall plan, the
kitchen will be expanded to accommodate the addittonal adult population. The
total cost of Phase 1 of the Covina projects is $7.7 million which will be financed
from the Masonic Homes General Fund. As in the Union City program, the

Due to the large number of applications in recent years, it became necessary to establis~ a wait~g list for admission to Union <;ity. In order to insure
tha-t those applicants with the most need would be admitted first, the Board of
Trustees developed a point rating system which would be sensitive to those
needs. This system provides the Board with a positive means to recognize the
IDOSt needy and place them in their proper place on the waiting list, regardless
of when they were approved for admission. This system recognizes the three
levels of care that we offer; Residential, Personal Care and Skilled Nursing, and
automatic.ally positions the most needy in each category as space becomes available in our Home: This system is constantly being reviewed for i~p~ovement.
An imp.roved version of this system has been developed by the Admissions Committee and will be used in the very near future.
Applications to the Children's Home in Covina are given the same careful
consideration as those for Union City. Since we are not operating near capacity,
it is not necessary to have a Point Rating System there.

ADMISSIONS TO HOMES
by Jack R. Vickers and Ralph M. Hinds, Co-Chairmen Admissions Committee
For many years the Board of Trustees operated without a formal Admissions Committee. This meant that each application for ad.mission to the
Masonic Home consumed a large portion of the meeting day because there
wasn't prior committee consideration. Subsequently, the Admissions Committee was established in order to maximize efficiency in OJ?erations of the Board
of Trustees. In so doing, the Board has been able to consider many applications
each month and provide sufficient attention to other important business matters of the Board.
The Board meets monthly, alternatin$ in the North at the Union City Home
and in the South at the Children's Home m Covina. The Admissions Committee has co-chairmen. Currently, Ralph M. Hinds serves as chairman in the
North and Jack R. Vickers as chairman in the South. They are supported by six
other members of the Board of Trustees; three each from the North and South.
The considered recommendations of the full committee are presented hy the
Chairmen to the Board for their approval.

The Personnel Committee recommended to the Board of Trustees a merit

were authonzed to grant pay increases to deserving employees.
The Masonic Homes Merit Program is based on these objectives:
To recognize differences in individual performance.
To provide monetary rewards for outstanding performers.
To mai~t.ain a pay system that is both internally fair and externally
compet1llve
A shortage of Registered and Licensed Nurses was experienced at the
Union City Home during this year. In order to assist in retaining our present
licensed staff, bring our rates of pay in line with similar industry, and attract
qualified applicants to fill existing and anticipated openings for R.N.'s and
L.V.N.'s a careful review of our nursing wage scale was necessary. With full
Board approval all Registered and Licensed Nursing positions were individually reviewed and adjusted to meet the competitive industry wage levels. The total
merit plan pool and special salary adjustment as outlined are provided for and
within the approved Masonic Homes Budget.

SUMMARY
Most Worshipful Jack R. Levitt, Grand Master, has the gratitude of the
Board of Trustees and the Brethren for his inspiring leadership and continuing
support.
John A. Sickenberger, Grand Treasurer, has served our Masonic Homes
with distinction. Our accounting and financial services reflect his knowledge
and abilities. His services have been invaluable.
Varnum Paul, Legal Counsel to the Board, continues to furnish sound legal
advice and assistance in the complex areas of management and government
regulations. He carries a heavy load of work on our behalf.
Chester R. MacPhee, P.G.M. and Hambleton F. Leas provide professional
services in the management and sale of real estate for the Homes.
Ronald A . Sherod, a professional in many areas of management, shares his
wealth of experience for the benefit of our two Homes. He has accepted many
assignments and made valuable contributions to the improvement of our operations.
Jack R . Vickers adds his analytical abilities to solve difficult problems and
reminds us of our charters as members of this Board.
Ralph M . Hinds has become an expert in the area of needs as reflected in
applications by our Brethren, widows and children for entrance into the Homes.
Stanley L. Channon, in spite of his extensive travel with the Elective Grand
Lodge Line, has fulfilled many import.a nt assignments. He has spent endless
time bringing our Union City and Covina expansion programs into being. We
are impressed with his attention to detail and his ability to lead.
Verl B. Lobb has developed an excellent publicity program. He has gained
the cooperation and confidence of everyone to make it a success.
Alvin J . Weis, Chairman of the Personnel Committee, and under his
guidance we have made many improvements in our policies and procedures.
He is a valuable member of this Board.
Richard S. Weber, who joined the Board this year, is a professional in the
areas of financial plannin~ and budget. We appreciate his experience and energy on behalf of the Masoruc Homes. Leo B. Mark, Stanley L. Channon and Sam
M. Pavlovich, in spite of heavy commitments as members of the Grand Lodge
Elective Line, have done their share within the limits of their schedules. The
Board has been supported and enriched by their dedication and talents.
Robert A. Klinger, Grand Secretary, and his staff, have given superb service to the Board of Trustees and to our two Homes.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

69

Hugo Z . Delfin and his accounting staff provided the accounting work and
financial reports so essential in the operation of the Homes.
Irene Harrigan and Corinne Conlon, who handle property transactions,
deserve our commendations for their outstanding work.
Sue Dean and Lynda Peyloclc, Homes Representatives, interview ai:
plicants and prepare their findings for the Board. We commend them for thetr
fine work.
Thanks to Administrator J. Burton Brown and his staff for providing the
love, care and security for our elderly at Union City.
Thanks to Administrator John A. Rose and his staff for providing the love,
patience and understanding for the care of our children at Covina.
As President of the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California, I thank the members of the Endowment Board for their outstanding efforts.
In addition, I also thank each member of the Board of Trustees for his complete
loyalty and dedication. We have never been blessed with finer talent nor greater
dedication. We are proud of each one of you and thank you for your contribution to the total effort on behalf of the Masonic Homes and the Brethren of this
Jurisdiction.
Finally, the Trustees pay the highest tribute to the Masons of California and
Hawaii for their continued support and confidence.

REPORT OF THE ADMINISTRATOR
COVINA HOME
1986-1987
It is with continued pleasure and commitment that this report is made to
the Grand Lodge.

COVINA EXPANSION
On March 1, 1987, a groundbreaking ceremony was held for the new
Masonic Home for Adults at Covina. The wisdom of older adults, the strength
and vitality of children, and the beauty of them all will soon adorn this Masonic
Home.
Your Administrator has been pleased to work with the Board of Trustees
in their professional planning and preparation for this Home for Adults soon
to be erected on this property. The administration of this new facility will be
jointly managed under one Director, although the housing and care programs
will be diverse and generally separate. This comingled use of common property will permit the utilization of present fixed costs of operation, thus reducing
the average cost per resident.

COVINA CHILDREN'S HOME
During this (.>ast year we have continued our dedicated work of providing
a family-like envuonment. Our child care program continues to address the
needs of the whole child. Our discipline and child care management systems
have been very effective. Requests from other Masonic Homes and Child Care
Institutions for our policies, procedures, training, personne~ and discipline systems suggest we are pacesetters in this philanthropy of child care.
Your Children's Home continues to monitor the determinant situations
within the extended family which resulted in the child(ren)'s placement. In
several situations, we have been effective in assisting a resident's return to his
family that is now able to meet his or her needs.
There is still evidence that many of our Fraternity members are not aware
of the admission criteria and application procedures of this Home. Still, and all
too often, it seems Masons believe the Masonic Home for children to be a home
for orphans, for boys only, or for the sons and daughters of Master Masons only.

85

It seems to be Masonry's best kept secret that the children served in this
Home are more often nieces, nephews, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren
of distressed Master Masons. It seems to be a secret that a great aim of the
Masonic Home is here to aid and assist those distressed Masons and their
families. Masons and their families should know this Home is here to help care
for their children in time of need.
The combination of our effective assistance with the extended family members and the lack of accurate information regarding the admission policies of
our Children's Home are directly related to our declining population. At fiscal
year end, we bad 30 boys and 16 girls for a total of 46 children. This is a decline
of 10.89% since last year.
Our youngest child is 5 years of age and the oldest is 18. We currently have
9 elementary students, 13, intermediate students, and 24 high school students.
Our residents continue their education through th~ublic school system in the
Charter Oak Unified School District.By and ihrou your example of Masonic
Charity, the following children have been served t is fiscal year:

MARCH I, 1987
GROUNDBREAKING CEREMONIES
FACILITY FOR THE ELDERLY AT COVINA
by
KERMIT A. JACOBSON, P.G.M.

President, Board of Trustees
Masonic Homes of California
Most Worshipful Jack R. Levitt, Grand Lodge Officers, Past Grand
Masters, Brethren, ladies, young people, and distinguished guests:
We welcome you to this special occasion for the ground breaking
ceremonies preparatory to the building of facilities for the care of our elderly.
We are hi~y honored to have the Most Worshipful Jack R. Levitt, Grand
Master and his corps of Grand Lodge Officers accept the invitation of your
Trustees to perform the ground breaking ceremonies.
As you know, the Masonic Homes of California is our non-profit corporation supported by the contributions from the members of the Grand Lodge of
Free and Accepted Masons of California and Hawaii, their families and related
Masonic Bodies.

87

We are proud to state for the record that our non-profit corporation does
not accept federal, state, county, or local financial assistance for the support of
our 88 year old charity.
Since 1899 the Masonic Home for Adults has been located solely in northern California in Union City and, at present, includes residential living, personal
care, and skilled nursing for some 400 elderly residents.
The Masonic Home for Children has also been in existence since 1899 and
was originally located in Union City with the adults.
The Children's Home, for various reasons, was relocated to a large tourist
hotel in the city of San Gabriel in 1909, and then to Covina in 1915 when the
building was severly damaged by flood waters.
Our Children's Home is older than the famed Boys' Town in Omaha,
Nebraska, and has raised nearly 1,800 children.
Graduates from the Home have become substantial members of society and
many are residents of the San Gabriel Valley.
Long range planning over the past five years by the Board of Trustees has
clearly indicated the need to expand our adult care facilities It has also indicated a desirability for residential facilities for the elderly in southern California
For various reasons over a number of years our Children's Home has experienced a declinin~ census. Your Trustees have been well aware of the large
fixed expenses associated with maintaining this 33 acre expanse of property for
a relatively few children.
This increased census which includes the elderly will allow us to share the
full campus and certain staff without an increase in present fixed costs. The annual cost per resident will be reduced to a more economical level.
Bringing the elderly and children in close proximity on this property is an
innovative and generally non-traditional approach lo adult living.
The first phase of the new construction will include 56 apartments, an ad~i~istralion buildin$ ~ith ~acilities. for various activities, a chapel, ~d main
dmmg room. Our eXIslmg kitchen will be expanded to accommodate mcreased
meal preparation and service. In phase 2 there will be an additional 56 apartments.
You are invited to review our artists' renderings and plans which are on display.
Each residential apartment will be approximately 700 square feet in size
and complete with kitchenette, living room, bedroom, bath, walk-in closet and
patio. Although the apartments are designed primarily for couples, the Maso nic
Home will serve single adults as well.
These two care programs for children and adults will be separate; however,
certain aspects will be merged. Worshipful John A. Rose, current Administrator of the Masonic Home for Children will assume the administrative
duties of this congregate living system.
Administration, physical plant, business and dietary will be commingled
services. Activities, transporation, dining, health, and residential care will be
generally separate and diverse.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

This proximity of living will {>rovide wonderful opportunities for chil~ren
and older adults to share in certain activities and events on a voluntary basts.
Young children and older adults compliment one another. Children
generally are not inhibited by age and do !lot placate older adults. The elderly
appreciate the sincerity and honesty of children.
Children look past wrinkles and recognize wisdom, value and worth. They
more often respect the elderly as wise members of society.
We envision certain adults volunteeri!lg to help children. in !11any ~ays. An
example mi~t be reading to th~ young c~.1ldren who are begummg therr learning. We enVtsion some olaer children domg the same for adults.
We can envision children and older adults fishing on the banks of our lake
in Rainbow Park.
Today we not only turn this first shovel of earth, but we signify a new begin. .
ning for Covina.
This also begins a time when the w;isdom of the elder_ly reaches out. ..JOms
hands with the youth ...and both are ennched by the expenence.

Master Mason, which is the trowel, is used because it is the trowel that spreads
the cement that binds that building into one common mass and makes it a building.

The wisdom of the elderly...
the strength and vitality of children ...
and the beauty of them both
will soon adorn this Masonic Home.

89

The lesson that we learn here is that the working tools of the first two
degrees teach us individually to be judicious in our time, to divest ourselves of
the superfluities of life and to walk uprightly and be square in our actions. But,
it's not until the sublime degree of Master Mason that we reach that of brotherly love, spreading love to others and so it exemplifies that principle of true
Masonic charity.
The building of a buildin~, and this building which will be built here, is going
to be the result of the spreading of the seeds which will bear the fruits of the future. Just as one casts a stone U(>On the placid surface of a body of water, the
disturbance goes out in greater crrcles, so if man could see after death what occurs on the earth, we here today would see in the future the ever-widening circles
of influence of good, of hundreds of our Brothers and their families who occupy
these buildings. We seek to commmence here the buildin~ of buildings which
are not merely temporal buildings, but buildings which will be safe havens of
love and comfort which will be given and shared.This is exemplifying the
Masonic principle, that no doctrine or faith or knowledge is of value to one unless it bears fruit or acation, or as the poet put it:
"It's not what you learn, and it's not what you teach.
It's not the things you remember, or the things you preach.

No, it's action that counts, not what's in your head.

MARCH 15, 1987
GROUNDBREAKING CEREMONIES
FACILITY FOR THE ELDERLY AT UNION CITY
ADDRESS OF WELCOME
by
KERMIT A. JACOBSON, P.G.M.

President, Board of Trustees
Masonic Homes of California
Today we stand on a part of the original 267 acres purchased in 1893 where
other Brother Masons have stood and participated in the same type ceremony.
The history of our Home here in Union City, or Decoto as many of us remember it, is laced with many such occasions.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

I wish to share with you an excerpt from the Home's Annual Report, dated
June 30, 1957. "We are facing a serious problem in relation to the almost capacity
population now at Decoto as there were only two vacancies for women, four for
men, and only one for a married couple. The hospital facility (as it was known
then) has been taxed during the past year--there appears to be no available
space in the p,resent building and the alternative is the erection of a new hospital building. The decision to resolve that problem was made the following year
and with an estimated cost of $1,000,000.00, the building you are facing became
a reality; our present Skilled Nursing Facility. Official groundbreaking
ceremonies took place on May 2, 1959, followed by the ceremony for laying the
comer stone on September 30th. Approximately 1400 members and ladies of
Grand Lodge attended as Most Worshipful Phil N. Myers, Grand Master, performed that importrant and significant task.
In 1962 the Board of Trustees dedicated that building to P.G.M. Charles
M. Wollenberg who served the Board as President from 1919 to 1959. The
dedication was made O ctober 10, during the visitation to the Home by Grand
Lodge. Most Worshipful Wollenberg died twelve days later, October 22, 1962.
So--today we are taking a page from our Masonic H ome history, whereby
the Board of Trustees find almost the identical situation existing.We, too, are
near our capacity of 167 in the Skilled Nursing Facility and realize that the need
for medical sefvices continues to be increasing throughout the population and
our own fraternal families. The informatio n on the inside of the program explains in some detail our plans for the use of the new building.
It is my pleasure to introduce the nephew of Hugo Lorber for whom this
addition will be named, Brother John Lorber and his wife Alice. John is a member of Menlo Park Peninsula Lodge No. 651.
In addition to this expansio n of the Skilled Nursing Facility, we are pleasedto symbolically break ~ound also for a magnificent building to be known as
Simmoff Center as depicted in the architect's renderings on display and shown
o n the cover of the program. Though there is little known of the history of the
Brother whose name has been identified with the Temple existing on this
property since 1903, Morris Siminoff was a member of Fidelity Lodge No. 120.
It was through his generous gift that the Simino ff Temple was erected and used
until 1976 when state officials deemed its construction did not meet current
earthquake standards. And, while we have no one representing the Siminoff
family, we ar e pleased to have the Master and Officers, and members of Fidelity
Lodge No. 120 here today.
I welcome each of you to this very special occasio n. Although we are not
1400 in number, we, too, as we participate with our G rand Master will be
recorded in the histsory of Masomc Homes of California.
We are hono red in having our Grand Master, Most Worshipful Jack R.
Levitt, and our elected and appointed Greand Lodge Officers accept the invitation of the Masonic Homes Board of Trustees to perform the groundbreaking
ceremonies for these new facilities. Again, we welcome you all on this happy
and historic occasion.

ANNUAL REPORT OF THE
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M . of California:
Your Masonic Homes Endowment Board is pleased to submit its 55th
Annual Report covering the fiscal year ending June 30, 1987. Through the
enthusiasm and dedication of the Board members and the continued commitment and support of the Brethren of this great Fraternity to the residents of our two Homes, contributions to the Endowment Fund have
exceeded one and one half million dollars.
INCOME FROM THE PERMANENT ENDOWMENT FUND

Income from the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund amounted. to
$5,214,415.94 which was transferred to the operating account of our two
Homes . This income is an extremely and vitally important factor in providing the Homes' Trustees with the funds necessary to maintain the exceptionally high quality of health care and services afforded to the residents
and to assist in providing for the future construction and enhancement of
the facilities at both of our Homes.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON DISTRIBUTION
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.&A.m. Of California
Your Committee on Distribution presents its report as follows:
GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE
There are four Recommendations and four Decisions contained in the
Grand Master's message to the Grand Lodge. Your Committee bas referred
these Recommendations and Decisions to the following Committees:
Recommendation No. 1 "Designation of Masonic Home at Covina" to the
Committee on Jurisprudence and also to the Masonic Homes Board of
Trustees.
Recommendation No. 2 "Delayed Installation of Grand Lodge Officers" to
the Committee of Jurisprudence, the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes and the Committee on Ritual.
Recommendation No. 3 "Elimination of Mandatory Appointment of Wardens to Grand Lod~e Committees" to the Committee on Jurisprudence the
Committee on Policy and General Purposes and the Special Committee
studying the Committee structure of Grand Lodge.
Recommendation No. 4 "Meeting Place of Masonic Lodges and Prerequisite Organizations" to the Committee on Jurisprudence, the Committee
on Policy and General Purposes, the Special Study Committee on Liquor
Laws, the Committee on Temple Properties and the Committee on Youth
Orders.
Decision No. 1 "Dispensation to Wear Masonic Regalia in Parades and at
Civic Events" to the Committee on Jurisprudence, the Committee on Policy
and General Purposes and the Committee on Ritual.
Decision No. 2 "Bank Credit Card Programs" to the Committee on
Jurisprudence and the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
Decision No. 3 "Construin~ Work of Improvement" to the Committee on
Jurisprudence, the Colllllllttee on Policy and General Purposes and the
Committee on Temple Properties.
Decision No. 4 "Shrine" the Committee on Jurisprudence and the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
GRAND TREASURER'S REPORT
We have referred the entire report of the Grand Treasurer to the Committee on Finance.
GRAND SECRETARY'S REPORT
We have referred the Grand Secretary's report to the following Committees:
That portion of the report relating to changes of meeting places of Lodges
to the Committee on Charters.

That portion of the report relating to the consolidation of Lodges to the
Committee on Charters.
That portion of the report relatin~ to "Exhibit A-Dispensations Issued and
Life Memberships" to the Comnuttee on Jurisprudence.
That portion of the report relating to "Exhibit B-Amendments to By-Laws"
to the Committee on By-Laws.
That portion of the report relating to "Exhibit C-Trial Records" to the Committee on Trial Review.
GRAND LECTURER'S REPORT

Report ADOPTED

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CHARTERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of Califomia:
At our 1986 Communication we informed you that three active Masonic
Clubs were meeting. Those Clubs have remained most active and all have made
excellent progress toward their goals of obtaining status as Lodges Under Dispensation.
Victor Valley Daylight Masonic Club in Victorville anticipates requesting
dispensation in 1988. Sunrise Masonic Club in Reseda is in the final stages of
preparing its request for dispensation and anticipates submitting that request
before the end of 1987. Three Stars Masonic Club in the San Diego area submitted their request for dispensation on September 3, 1987. The Charters Committee on September 9, 1987 recommended to G rand Master Levitt that the
Three Stars Masonic Club be granted the status of Three Stars Lodge U.D.
A group of dedicated Brethren in Temecula on July 1, 1987 formed the
Temecula Masonic Club. These Brethren have demonstrated their ability and
dedication to their goal of establishing a new Lodge in an area with rapidly expanding population and many sojourners where there are no other Masonic
Lodges within a radius of fifteen miles or more.

COMMITIEE ON RECOGNITION OF
FOREIGN GRAND LODGES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
There has been a continuation of the adverse publicity given Freema.sonry
worldwide. Some bodies of the Methodist Church, for instance, have contmued
the policy of regarding Masonry as being "incompatible with C~ristianity". This
attitude has seemed to encourage some groups not recogmu:d. as re~lar
Masonic organizations to increase their pressure for su~h rccogruhon. It is the
opinion of this Committee that now is not a time to sublillt to such pressure, but
to be ever more on guard, and to even more carefully ~crutinize su~h re.quests.
Conversely, egual attention and concern must be given to cons1dermg the
legitimating of properly qualified groups.

122

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The ongoing Masonic situation in Italy has consumed much time and attention for several years now. It appears from the recognjtion statement of the
Grand Orient of Italy that it is complying with all the re9uisites. There is, in the
opinion of the Commission of Informatton for Recogrution, definite improvement in concerned areas by the Grand Orient, but there remains a split in
opinjon as to whether it should be given recognjtion. Your Committee recommends prudence and to wajt for developments which may be more illuminating
by the next Grand Masters Conference.
The Grand Lodge of Greece has undergone some tribulations due to the
schism created by a new organization breaking away, calling itself the National
Grand Lodge of Greece, and applying for separate recognition. Our Grand
Lodge has received such application. However, the Grand Lodge of Greece is
recognized by all the Grand Lodges of the United States and the Commission
has made a thorough study of the situation and "--sees no reason to change its
opinion that the Grand Lodge of Greece is regular and entitled to continued
recognition." We concur in this finding.
The Benito Juarez Grand Lodge of Mexico has by letter applied to our
Jurisdiction for recognition. Some thirteen American Grand Lodges recognize
this small body, notable among them, the Grand Lodge of Texas. Members of
this foreign Grand Lodge are reported to be enthusiastic and sincere Masons,
deserving of recognition. We recommend recognition.
There is no change in the status of the (new) Grand Lodge of Iran which
was constituted in New York in 1983. Massachusetts continues to be the only
Grand Lodge which permits them to operate as a Grand Lodge in exile. According to R.W.Robert Dillard, Jr., the group consists of some very fme men
who are doing a good job under trying circumstances.However, due to the long
and Masonically complicated history of this troubled group from a troubled
country, your Committee doubts that our Grand Lodge should change its attitude of watchful waiting at thjs time.
Much effort has been properly made in the past to accommodate Iranian
Masons for purpose of affiliation wtth regular North American Lodges but there
has also been confusion created by the desire of some of the Iranian representatives to full right of visitation and establishment of their own Lodges under
their own Grand Jurisdiction. The policy of clearing applications for affiliation
through the Grand Secretary before reception seems an appropriate method of
serving the good Masons oflranian descent in California.
We have received a communication from a group calling itself the Gran
Logia Equinoccial Del Ecuador in Quito to initiate fraternal recognjtion. The
recognized Grand Lodge of Ecuador is located in Guayaquil and claims jurisdiction over the entire Republic of Ecuador and advises that it has not changed
its constitution to allow the formation of a Grand Lodge in Quito and has not
surrendered its jurisdiction in any way. The so-called Grand Lodge in Quito
should therefore, not be considered regular.
The Grand Lodge of Peru, recognized by all North American Grand Jurisdictions, re{>Orts an extraordinary session of the Executive Committee of the
Inter-Amencan Masonic Federation, in Lima, Peru, to deal with a Masonic
jurisdictional dispute in Colombia. We await the outcome.

REPORT OF CREDENTIALS COMMITTEE

GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. &A.M. of California:
Your Committee on Credentials is pleased to submit this report of the 138th
Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge.
Again we wish to express our thanks to the Grand Secretary and his office
for their help.
Of the 571 chartered Lodges, 526 are represented, as is 1 U.D. Lodge.
The total registration is as follows:

My Brethren:
I am before you to present for your approval an account of my official acts
during the year, to exhibit the general conditions of Masonry within the Jurisdiction, and to recommend such legislation as I deem expedient for the welfare
of the Craft. The nature and extent of the functions of the office of Grand
Master are so vast that no one can truly measure up to the full standard set by
the honor, dignity and importance of the office. I have enlisted in your service
every faculty I possess, and have diligently and painstakingly striven to meet
every demand with devotion and zeal. Whatever history shall judge of my efforts, I shall always be blessed with recurring joy by being able to reminisce over
the pleasure of association this past year with so many fine Brethren, their
families and friends.
Evolution takes place under the alternation of forces which require a constant adjustment between seemingly competing, but, in actuality complimentary
forces -- the material and the spiritual. In any age when materialism is pushed
to excess, there is a tendency toward a revival of the spiritual.
I believe such a time bas arrived, and that the Fraternity of Free and Accepted Masons is ready, once again, to provide the moral and spiritual foundation to such a revival. I have come to appreciate the importance for all
Freemasons to realize how unifying our great Fraternity is. All men are akin,
not only in origin, but in desire and destiny. Men want more and better material
possessions and greater comfort, but they need more to know and love each
other. Freemasonry bring.s together men of every rank and walk of life, where
they can share the views and experiences of each other, soothe each other's
troubles and meet together in an atmosphere devoid of conflict and strife.
Being a Freemason is a very precious thing. To belong to an organization
that re moves misunderstandings between men, makes them friends, and teaches
them to love one another, is to possess something that cannot be measured in
understandable terms. We should encompass it, savor it, and protect it.
Our desrees give us a picture of human life from birth of intellectual light
to the acquisition of the Perpetual Light which eminates from the Sanctum
Sanctorum; a path of progress from the ignorance of infancy to the wisdom of
maturity; an answer to why we are here and where we are ~oing and a series of
guideposts to show the way to find the lost Word. Behmd the ceremonies,
doctnne and symbols of Freemasonry there is a spiritual side, which offers, in
dramatic form, a philosophy of the spiritual side of man, and a diagram of the
process of regeneration.
Our great Fraternity is the oldest and largest in the world. It has drawn man
to it across the centuries from every culture. It is a mine of wealth containing a
distillation of the wisdom of the ages and a legacy of leaching.s to assist us to
come to terms with moral order and design within a potentially cold and heartless universe. It provides the path toward moral and spiritual progress,
knowledge, and service of God and our fellow men. It causes us to stand apart
from all other Fraternal orders. We have every reason to be optimistic that our
Craft will be just as viable 100 years from now as it was 100 years ago, and that,
eventually, all men the world over will learn to know and love each other at the
altar of Freemasonry.
