CONDITION OF THE CRAFT

These letters illustrate that personal interest shown in a Brother is not only
the extension of a helping hand, but is a continuance of that spark of brotherly
love that attracted the Brother to our Fraternity.
lnterest in the personal welfare of, and continual contact with, our Brethren
cannot be stressed enou~. Most men who do not continue their membership
express lack of concern 6y Lodge Brothers as the principal reason. Remember
that we are to aid, support and protect, as well as to sympathize with each other's
misfortunes and compassionate each other's misenes. Remember also, that to
devote an immense amount of time to the work of initiating, passing and raising Masons, but failin~ to instruct or help, or minister to our mernbers, places
us in danger of becommg patrons of the mediocre, who will not be able to retain
the attention or the membership of those we originally attract.

The year now closing has been one of great activity and of great apathy. In

seeming inexplicable contrast, some Lodges are in a precarious condition, while
others are prospering. Consolidations are on the rise, while at the same time
some Lodges are increasing in membership and enthusiasm. Everywhere there
are contrary circumstances1 for example, some Lodges having mostly older
members and others attracting younger ones.
In times like these, it is well to remember that there have always been times
like the.se.Jn reading through the Proceedings of the Grand Lodge of California, from before the turn of the century to the present, one can find references
by Grand Masters to: Consolidation problems; The need for greater educational and social functions on the part of Lodges; O vere mphasis on ritual; Incidents
of petty character; Membership concerns; Poor attendance; and Financial distress.
I am convinced that by accentuating the positive and appealing for a new
sense of duty and a fuller consecration to the eternal ideals of Brotherly Love,
Relief and Truth we will keep the sacred fire, the abiding, immutable, divine essence of Freemasonry strong and viable and available to those who, in the future, seek the Word and the Light that shines in the East.
MEMBERSHIP
Every Mason should, at all times, extend the hand of Brotherly Love to
every other Mason. Because our Lodges are oases of serenity in a desert of strife,
because men need love and understanding and fellowship far more than
material gains, and, because we offer a sanctuary from the controversial matters upon which differing opinions can be held without rancor, our great Fraternity should attract and keep good men of every persuasion and background. It
is a privilege to be a Freemason. Not everyone who knocks on our door is
granted admission. Retention of members is as important as their acquisition.
To impress these thoughts, and encoura~e maintenance of membership, I have
sent congratulatory letters to all newly initiated Entered Apprentice Masons indicating they have joined a Fraternity, well known for its moral and and
philosophical principles and for extending charity and good will to all people.
This letter informed them that advancement through the remaining degrees will
bring them much pleasure, satisfaction and Masonic education. In an endeavor
to further convince them that advancement is essential, the letter emphasized
that we value those things which we earn more than those things which are given
us, and that what they learn through coaching and the remaining degrees,
coupled with the fellowship and the satisfaction they will obtain, is something
they will treasure all their hfe. It is hoped that this letter has influenced most of
them to progress on to become Master Masons.
I have also sent letters to all Masons who have requested a dim.it, as well as
to those who are in arrears in Lodge dues and subject to being suspended. These
letters remind them that they have spent considerable time, effort, and money
in becoming a Master Mason, and, that they are giving up the rights and benefits
that Freemasonry has to offer. These letters suggest their situation is of great
concern and if there are circumstances that have brought them to request a
<limit, or that prohibit them from paying dues, such could be discussed m confidence. As a result, many Brothers have brought their dues current and many
have withdrawn their requests for <limits.

SOJOURNERS
The number of sojourners in California is unknown, but estimated to be in
the many, many thousands. A great number of these Brothers would attend
Lodges in our Jurisdiction, and perhaps affiliate , but probably are concerned
at not being able to pass an examination for admittance. To overcome this
reticence, the Sojourners Committee, in addition to its other efforts regarding
sojourners has developed the "Rusty Trowel Ceremony". This ceremony, which
carefully screens those involved, demonstrates enough of "the work" to provide
reasonable certainty of being able to pass a private examination. Encouraging
reports are being made by Lodges which have used this ceremony indicating
that affiliations of sojourners are a result. The Committee is putting together a
booklet covering the entire sojourner program and how to put it into execution,
which will be distributed when completed.
LODGE SYSTEM OF CANDIDATE INFORMATION
The importance of Masonic Education to the future of Freemasonry is evident. Masonic education is one of the factors necessary to carry Freemasonry
forward. Together with ritual, it is essential to adequately convey to our candidates, as well as our established members, the moral, philosophical and
religious principles taught by our symbols and allegories. Freemasonry has both
an outer, visible aspect and an inward, hidden one. The visible aspect conveys
the moral and ethical principles, but the hidden one is full freighted with
philosophy, and intellectual wisdom. Seldom do we employ our Lodges for that
purEse, which, as much as for ceremonial purposes, they were intended -- i.e.
for expatiating on the mysteries of the Craft".
In January a letter was sent to all Masters urging them to appoint a Masonic
educator and encouraging them to set up and coordinate Masonic education in
their Lodges. In April another letter was sent to all Masters strongly requesting them to initiate the "Lodge System of Masonic Information for Candidates"
by appointing a member as a "Lodge Counselor" to be Chairman of the Lodge's
Masonic Education program. I herein continue to solicit each Lodge to establish a Masonic education program, or strengthen its existing one, as it is essential to educate our members in the deeper meaning and true purpose of our
rites and its philosophy.

I am pleased to report that the 1987 Public Schools Week programs
throughout the Jurisdiction were generally successful. I had the pleasure of attending the program co-sponsored by U niversity Lodge No. 394 and Torrence
Lodge No. 447. This was a splendidly run and well attended event. Many members of the School Board and City Council, the Mayor, and a large number of
teachers and school administrators were in attendance. There was much enthusiasm from the large gathering of students and parents, who showed much
favorable appreciation. I commend this program as a model to our Lodges and
suggest contact with either Lodge for specifics.
Our Grand Lodge became involved in awarding savings bonds to winners
of essay contests on the United States Constitution, conducted by the California State D epartment of Education in conjunction with the Commission on the
Bicentennial of the United States Conslit ution and others. There were contests
at the High School and elementary school level. We presented bonds to 13 winners who had written on the topics, "Wbat the Constitution means to Me and to
Our Country" and "Does the Separation of Powers help make it work?" These
bonds were presented by our Constituent Lodges in their communities.
Increased community activity in this and other areas is essential not only
for public relations, but because our Masonic influence is required to bolster
those non-Masons who nonetheless think and live Masonic pnnciples.

ROSE PARADE FLOAT
1987 marked the first year in its 137 year history that the Grand Lodge of
California sponsored a float in the Annual Tournament of Roses Parade in
Pasadena.
The principal purpose fo r it was to call attention to the American Constitution and the support Freemasonry gives to it. It was especially appropriate to
emphasize that 1987 was the Bicentennial of the signing of the Constitution, a
truly unique document of personal freedom and one of the wonders of the
world.
The float represented "Liberty, Peace and Equality". Sixty-five feet in
length, it was designed with three huge American eagles in full flight. The first
eagle, with its wing tips reaching a height of 28 feet, had its talons resting upon
a replica of the Liberty Bell, representing "Liberty". The second eagle carried
in its beak garlands of palm leaves, representing "Peace". The third eagle with

132

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

talons resting upon the scroll of the Constitution represented "Equality". The
base o[ red roses represented America's fertile lands, and the stars springing
forth from the base of red roses represented the fifty States of the Uruon.
Several foreign national flags on the float were symbolic of the fact that the
United States Constitution served as a model not only for all fifty of our States,
but also Canada, Mexico, five Republics of Central America, nine Republics of
South America, Australia, France, ·Belgium, Union of South Africa and Switzerland.
Riding upon the float, wearing Masonic aprons and representing all
Masons in California and Hawai~ were three pronunent members of the Fraternity: Brothers Ernest Borgnine, Norman Crosby, and Royal Dano. In addition,
Brother Joe Dines was dressed as George Washington and wore a replica of
the original apron worn by that eminent Mason and President of the United
States.
The float was decorated entirely by members of the California Youth
Groups: the International Order of De Molay, the International Order of Job's
Daughters, and the International Order of the Rainbow for Girls. These young
people worked tirelessly over many days and hours lo complete the float. Under
the chairmanship, tireless efforts and inspiring guidance of Most Worshipful H.
Douglas Lemons, Past Grand Master, this beautiful float was created, and,
through personal attendance at the parade and television, was viewed by literally millions of peo ple. From reports received after the parade, many thousands
of Masons' hearts beat with pride and joy on New Year's Day, 1987.
I have prcviouslx expressed my gratitude to all who labored on behalf of
this historic and sigmficant event. I again do so by publicly acknowledging that
they truly and materially assisted the cause of Freemasonry.
In addition to the Grand Lodge Float in the Rose Parade, the Lodges of
our Jurisdiction organized and participated in various pr~rams and parades
celebrating the Bicentennial of the United States Const1tullon. In excess of 80
dispensations were issued to allow our members to march and appear in public
in aprons and Masonic regalia.
Early in the year, the California Bicentennial Foundation for the United
States Constitution sou~ht the assistance of the Freemasons in California in organizing California's Bicentennial. Since this afforded us a challenge to help
our Country and also to further demonstrate that Masons have respect for the
Constitution of the United States, it was considered desirable to urge our members to demonstrate the support of the Fraternity to the Bicentennial celebration in every appropriate way. One of its efforts was the National Constitution
Day Banner project desi~ed to have supporting organizations present a red,
white and blue Constitution Day Banner to city or community officials, and to
display like banners in front of homes and businesses during September. Early
in July, 1 sent a letter to every Master informing them of the Foundation's National Constitution Day Banner project and encoura~n~ cooperation, as well
as indicating that participation in it would be a Const1tullon week program.

January 5, 6, and8, February 9, 25, and March 19 and 23, 1987, all of which permitted the sale, serving, or use of alcohol in its buildings in knowing violation of
California Masonic Law.
Thereafter , I summo ned appropriate representatives of Al Malaikah
T emple, includin$ its Recorder and its Potentate, to attend a meeting on April
26, 1987, to explain to them the potential conse9uences of their past and continued violations of the law. After much discussion and threats by them to execute further leases involving liquor, an<l with great reluctance on their part,
bordering on defiance, especially on the part of the Potentate and Recorder,
the following agreement was entered into:
1. All violations because of written leases which involved the use or sale of
alcohol, completed prior to April 26, 1987, would be exempted from any
punitive action by the Grand Lodge; in exchange for which
2. The Temple would not again enter into any lease agreements wherein alcohol is to be used, served or sold.
Similar negotiatio ns occurred with the Potentate of Aloha Temple, who iriformed me that many commitments had been made for the future use of the
Temple's country ho me property, which wo uld include the serving and selling
of alcoholic beverages. I requested the Po tentate to seek avoidance of as many
as possible. He did so, which resulted in most of such potential users being able
to use alternate facilities or holding events on the Shririe prope rty without alcoholic beverages. In exchange for assurance that henceforth the California
Masonic Code would be strictly observed, and, in light of the good faith effo rts
made to eliminate the pending code violatio ns, I aweed to impose no Masonic
penalties on the uses v.ith alcoholic beverages which had been, as well as the
few which we re thereafter, carried out by Aloha T emple.
An inordinate amount of time has been spent during this last Masonic year
by your G rand Master, the Jurisfrudencc Committee, the Commercialism
Committee, the other members o the Executive Committee, Inspectors and
others because of the attitude and activities of the leaders of most of the Shrine
T emples.
I exceedingly regret that so much time and energy was diverted from constructive and forward efforts on behalf of our beloved Fraternity. Upon reflection, it is of greater regret to realize that any member of the Fraternity of Free
and Accepted Masons, who voluntarily and willingly took an oath on the H oly
Bible and swore befo re his God, could violate his oath so cavalierly. Unfortunately, some of o ur Brethren consider themselves to rate an exemptio n fro m
the provisions of the California Masonic Code, or detcrmfoe to violate it in wanton disregard of their hono r. They must come to the realization that they are
like all other Masons and not above the law, and should ask themselves the questio n --"What will it profiteth a man if he shall gain the whole world and lose bis
own Soul?".
We have the right to demand from our members deeds of principle and integrity rather than the ne_g)i$encc of iridifference or the treason of violations.
Our great Order has at all times religio usly preserved the teachings of moral
self-respect and faithfulness to its trusts and ideals.

HIRAM AWARD
The Hiram Award was promulgated in 1979 as a constituent Lodge
program to honor the unsung and non-recognized workers in the quarry. Its intent was to give special recognition to the Brother who has worked tuelessly
and without reward. It was contemplated that the Brothers qualified for this
unique, and hopefully cherished, honor would be those who had contributed
over a long period of time, and, who had not otherwise received Masonic recognition. It was also contemplated that the honor would be given sparingly and
selectively, so as not to dilute its worth. Attention to these guidelines wiT! make
its giving and receiving meaningful.

SISTERS OF HIRAM CLUBS
It came to my attention that there were various Sisters of Hiram clubs in
existence in the Jurisdiction of our Grand Lodge. Such are neither concordant
nor prerequisite organizations, and, henee, not subject to the jurisdiction of the
Grand Lodge of California. However, in many of the cases, the charters had
been attested to by Masters of Constituent Lodges. Although Masons, as individuals, may provide all the individual support they wish for such organizations, Lodges may not subsidize them, and no Lodge funds may be expended
for such clubs, nor is it a proper Masonic activity for either a Constituent Lodge
or the Grand Lodge of California to give such clubs recognition.
RESOLUTIONS DECLARED OUT OF ORDER
Two Resolutions, timely submitted, were ruled out of order, after consultation with, and concurrence of, the members of the Committee on
Jurisprudence.
The first would have mandated the Grand lodge to cause a ritual cifher
book to be written and printed. Because this would necessitate violation o the
obli~ations each Mason takes, it was determined that no one could implement
it without being subjected to the penalties that pertain to an act of unmasonic
conduct.
The second sought to have incorporated into the California Masonic Code
the Constitution and all the laws of the United States and the Constitution and
all the laws of the State of California. In the introductory portion of the proposed
Resolution, the proponent suggested, among other things, that the Grand
Lodge have the same system of voting as both houses of the Congress of the
United States and of the fifty States therein. Notwithstanding numerous efforts
to ascertain the intent of the proponent, so that appropriate le~lation could
be drafted, the only response by him was the simplistic one to "incorporate all
the laws of the Constitution of the United States and the laws of the State of

Section 1310 be amended by deleting from the first sentence the words
"Home for Children at Covina and the Home at Union City", and substituting
in lieu thereof, the words "Masonic Homes".
Recommendation No. 2 - Installation of Grand Lodge Officers.
Section 200 of the California Masonic Code provides that the Elective Officers shall be installed before the close of Grand Lodge. While it has not happened, there exists the potential that a Grand Lodge officer could be elected
but not be installed before the close of the Annual Communication due to sudden iJlness, a family emergency, etc. A reasonable interpretation of Section 200
is that the person holding the office to which such absent Brother has been
elected would remain in that position until his successor was elected and installed at the next Annual Communication. This could result in a Grand Lodge
officer serving in two elected positions at the same time for an entire Masonic
year.
To correct this situation, I recommend that Section 200 of the California
Masonic Code be amended to delete the entire next to last sentence and substitute in its stead the following:
"The Elective Officers shall be installed before the close of the Annual
Communication, provided, however, that if an Elective Officer is unable to
be present, due to circumstances beyond his control, he may be installed
by the Grand Master at an appropriate place, with such ceremony as
deemed proper by the Grand Master, as soon as practicable following the
close of the Annual Communication, not to exceed sixty days. If the Elective Officer is not installed within such sixty days, the office shall be declared
vacant and the Grand Master may appoint any member of Grand Lodge to
fill the vacant Elective Office from time to time, or for the remainder of the
Grand Lodge year."

Recommendation No. 3 - Appointment of Senior and Junior Wardens to
Grand Lodge Committees
The Special Study Commission on Grand Lodge Committee Structure
recommends that Section 1202 of the California Masonic Code be amended to
eliminate, or at least make optional, at the discretion of the Grand Master, that
provision requiring the appomtment of one Senior Warden and one Junior Warden on Standing Committees of more than five members. The reasoning of the
Commission is tbat: the first obligation of the Wardens of any constituent Lodge
is to attend and represent their Lodge on the floor of Grand Lodge; and to place
a Warden on a working committee which must of necessity absent itself from
the floor during the Annual Communication, puts the Lodge, which the Warden represents, at a distinct disadvantage, since his attention is diverted to some
parochial aspect of Grand Lodge, rather than to observing and participating in
the overall discussions, transaction of business and debate of the Annual Communication.
I have discovered that, in addition to this reasoning, many Wardens express
the desire not to serve as they are too busy with the ritual and administrative
aspects of their constituent Lodges. I have also discovered that it is impracticable and, perhaps, harmful to the Craft to appoint some Senior Wardens in

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

141

October because they then become Masters within the next several months and
are eith~r unwilling to serve in both capacities or at least a substantial burden
is placed upon the Master.
Accordingly, I am of the view that appoin~ment o~Senior and Junior Wardens on Standing Committees should be optional with the Grand Master. I
therefore recommend that Section 1202 A of the California Masonic Code be
amended as follows: in the fourteenth line after the words Junior Warden the
word "shall" be eliminated and that there be substituted in lieu thereof the words
"in the discretion of the Grand Master may", and that Section 1202 B of the
California Masonic Code be amended as follows: to eliminate the second sentence thereof.

Decision No. 2 - Commercialism

Members of several organizations in our Jurisdiction requiring Masonic
membership as a prerequis ite were solicited throughout this and previous years
to join various bank credit card pr?Wams. California Masonic Code Section
2070 forbids any Lodge or prerequis ite organization in our Jurisdiction from
undertak ing any commercial venture, whether for profit or not, which shall not
first have been approved by the Grand Master. Likewise, neither the Lodge nor
the prerequis ite or~anization's name and/or symbol may be used on business
cards (which would mclude a bank card if used for a business purpose) , nor may
the roster of such organization be used for other than a strictly Masonic purpose. After consulta tion with the Committ ees on Commer cialism and
Jurisprud ence, I determin ed that approval of such programs should be given
only upon condition that no Masonic fraternal emblem, logo, or name of any
Masonic fraternal organization, subor~anization, or charity appear on any card
issued to a Mason subject to the jurisdiction of our Grand Lodge, and that only
members of the ~rerequisite organization issuing the cards participate in the
program. According]y, I granted approval of bank card programs, upon such
condition, to the. Kmghts Te.mplar Eye Foundation, Inc.; Supreme Council
Grottos of North America; Islam and Al Malaikah Temples, AA.O.N. M.S.;
and the Southern and Northern Masonic Jurisdiction Ancient and Accepted
Scottish Rite.
It is therefore my Decision No. 2 that bank card program solicitation may
take place in this J unsdiction only with the approval of the Grand Master, and
upon condition that as a result no Masonic fraternal emblem, logo, or name of
any Masonic fraternal organization, suborganization or charity be imprinte d
upon any bank card issued to a Mason subject to the Jurisdiction of the Grand
Lodge of California.

Decision No. 3 -Approval of Replacement Work by Temple Properties Committee
Jn July, 1987, the Capital City Masonic Temple Association asked for a
determin ation as to whether certain proposed roofing and gutter work to be ac-

complished by it required the prior approval of the Committ ee on Temple
Properties. Section 1208 of the Califorma Masonic Code preclude s contractm g
for, or commencing the "construction, alteration, or improvement" of a Masonic
Temple, the cost of which is in excess of $5,000.00, without first obtaining the
approval of the Committee on Temple Properties.
The only reported prior interpretation of "alteration" is annotation 1208b
which provides that the purchase of a new carpet is not an alteration of the building. That interpret ation was made in 1955, however, when the applicable section contained reference only to a Masonic Temple "to be erected or altered"
rather than to "construction, alteration or improvement" as in the present Section.
I determin ed that it was the intent of Section 1208 to require approval only
of construction alterations or improvements which change the structura l aspect
of a Masonic Temple, and that the proposed roofing and gutter work was not
in this category, as it was for the purpose or replacem ent only.

144

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Therefore, it is my Decision No. 3 that approval of the Committee on
Temple Properties need not be first obtained before contracting for or commencing any work or improvement (such as roof and gutter replacement) which
does not alter or add to the structural aspect of a Masonic Temple.
Decision No. 4 - Shrine
At the 1987 Imperial Session, the Ancient Arabic Order Nobles of the Mystic Shrine, amended subsections (e) and (t) of Section 323.8 of Article 23 of the
By-laws of its Iowa Corporation concerning retention of membership. The
amendment allows a member who loses his membership in a prerequisite body,
for any reason other than non-payment of dues, to appeal to the Imperial Council. If the Imperial Council determines the reason for loss of membership is not
a violation of Shrine law, the man, although suspended or expelled from the prerequisite organization, will retain membership in his Shrine Temple.
The effect of the Amendment is to permit a man who bas been expelled by
his constituent Lodge, and thus expelled from the bodies prerequisite to Shrine
membership, to continue membership in hisSb.rine Temple, and to attend meetings of his own and other Sh.cine Temples, if exonerated by the Shrine. In short,
the effect is to allow non-Masons to sit in tiled meetings of the Shrine with
Masons. Hence the Shrine has undertaken to substitute its own determination
in place and instead of the result of the constituent Lodge trial.
Section 100 of the California Masonic Code provides that "the Grand Lodge
is the Supreme Masonic Power and Authority in this Jurisdiction and is vested
with all legislative, executive, and judicial powers, limited only by a strict adherence to the Ancient Landmarks of the Order, and by the provisions of its
own Constitution and Regulations.".
Under Section 7 of the California Masonic Code, "The Jurisdiction of the
Grand Lodge includes all .L odges and Masons within the territorial limits of this
State, all Lodges and their members without this State, actin~ under its
authority, and members of Lodges of this jurisdiction wherever residing".
Section 2032 of the California Masonic Code forbids any member of a constituent Lodge from holding Masonic intercourse with an expelled or suspended
Mason.
Under Section 2612 of the California Masonic Code "All members of organizations within this territorial ju.risdiction of the Grand Lodge, the prerequisite of membership wherein is that a person be a Master Mason, shall be
subject to the same standards of conduct and propriety as are or may be imposed upon Master Masons in this Jurisdiction."
Because this amendment of its By-laws by the Shrine very seriously infringes upon the inte.grity of Freemasonry and the jurisdiction of our Grand
Lodge, I issued the following edict which constitutes my Decision No. 4.
FRATERNAL NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN pursuant to the authority
vested in me by Sections 7, 100, 106 and 300 of the California Masonic Code,
that commencing forthwith and so Ion$ as any Temple of the Ancient and AcceI?ted Order Nobles of the Mystic Shnne ("Shrine") in California or Hawaii requires Masonic membership, either directly or indirectly, as a prerequisite to
its membership:

This year we have been emphasizing the positive and the need to eliminate
the negat1ve. The enthusiasm and optimism, and all of the visions, the efforts
and the accomplishments of this past memorable year we share together as
Brethren. By the finalization of this Masonic year, as by the tum of a season, the
end of a storm, or by the consummation of some eventful period, we are
reminded th~t the time has come for. a re-awakenin~. To. renew .or str~ng_then
our interest m Freemasonry and to sip afresh from its re1uvenatmg pnnc1ples
can be the beginning of a new outlook on life. We must take hold of our Masonry apply our gifts and talents and work with dedication and self-discipline. We
m~st also have high expectations for ourselves and our Brethren and convert
every challenge into an opportunity. Freemasonry is, in the fmal analysis, to be
judged by the associations, dee.els, words, and conduct of its members. It is how
we each think in our heart that will dictate the course of our action.
Because we never invite anyone to come to our altars, our mental attitudes
and physical activities and our influence in the community must inform Godbelieving men of the mission of our Order. It is up to each of us to energize ourselves and to exemplify the faith of Freemasonry, so that others might look to
us for example and inspiration, and thus spread Freemasonry's plea for universal friendship and its concern for human progress.
Let us go forward in the years to come as partners in a Fraternity which
seeks to turn men toward truth, righteousness and character, to assist them in
chan~g doubt to faith, d espair to hope and fear to courage, and whose mission 1t is to cause men to know, understand and love each other. Let us above
all live in a manner befitting the dignity and worth of the Soul, remembering, as
Emerson said, that "what lies behind us and what lies before us are tiny matters
compared with what lies within us".
Continue the Mystic Quest and find peace and rest!

ACKNOWLEDGMENTS
With deep meaning, I offer my gratitude to the Great Architect of the
Universe for the strength to have performed my duties and the blessing of wisdom to have carried out my responsibilities as Grand Master. I cannot adequately express how much I am beholden for the Divine guidance I received this
past year.
The significant contributions lo Freemasonry and our Grand Lodge this
year by so many dedic.ated, selfless Brethren cannot adequately be addressed.
I simply here state my thanks for all the support, encouragement, assistance,
dedication and tireless work provided by so many. I am confident that those
who are deserving of praise are of the quality of char a.c ter that. they have served
without hope of recognition, and with the understanding that the self-knowledge
they have contributed is their sufficient, even if it be their sole, reward.
While I shall be eternally grateful to them, as well as all Brethren who
thought and acted as true Freemasons during this past year, I will without meaning to diminish any other's contributions, reference two people in particular.
One is Most Worshipful Donald B. Mc Caw, Past Grand Master, as Chairman
of the Committee on Jurisprudence, for his always available calm, sound advice
and incalculatable expenditure of time, energy and thought. It is men of his
calibre that must have inspired the poem by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow:
"The heights by great men reached and kept
Were not attained by sudden flight,

147

\

But they, while their companions slept
Were toiling upward in the night".
The other is my supl?ortive wife, Kay, who was an endless source of inspiration, a constant eompamon, a needed morale builder, and for whom I shall always have a silent, unspeakable love.
CONCLUSION
In seeking lo bring this message to a close and indkate my thoughts for the
privilege of serving as your Grand Master, I know how Lord T ennyson must
have felt when, looking at the sea and listening to its voices, he wrote "I would
that some tongue could utter the thoughts that arise in me". Even if I had the
speaking or writing acumen of an oratorical or literary ~enius, I would fall short
of being able to portray my sense of pride for your haVtng bestowed on me the
high honor to serve in this truly exalted station.

Our procedure now requires the appointment of one Senior Warden and
one Junior Ward~n to standing committees of more than five (5) members.
Among the good things to be said for appointment of Wardens as committee members are these:
1. They contribute new ideas.
2. They contribute the thinking of those less exposed to Grand Lodge.
3. They take back to their Lodges new insight and experience.
The Grand Master has recited the things which sometimes make it difficult
to appoint Wardens.
We appreciate the fact that Wardens' time as Wardens after appointment,
is short lived.
Another difficulty is finding Wardens qualified for specific .C<?mmittee
responsibilities. We believe that objection can be overcome by obtatrung more
information about Wardens.
We believe the general pur(>9ses and P-Qlicies of the Grand Lodge are better served by the continued requirement of appointment of Wardens.
The Policy and General Purposes Committee recommends a "No" vote.
The Special Committee ap;:>ointed to study the committee structure of
Grand Lodge recommended a Yes" vote.
Recommendation HELD OVER.

DECISION NO. 1
DISPENSATION TO WEAR MASONIC REGALIA
IN PARADES AND AT CIVIC EVENTS.
The Committee on Jurispmdence:
Your Committee on J urisprudcnce to which Grand Master's Decision No.
1 has been referred, reports as follows:
The Grand Master has interpreted Section 2058 of the California Masonic
Code to authorize Grand Masters to approve Applications for Dispensation by
Lodges to allow the wearing of station a_prons, officers' jewels, and Masters' top
hats as a part of Masonic regalia in puolic processions and at public meetings
and places.
Your Committee on Jurisprudence reports that this Decision of the Grand
Master is consistent with our 1aw and does not require an amendment to the
California Masonic Code. As a result, a majority vote only is required to approve the Decision of the Grand Master.
:r.o place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the approval of the
Decis10n.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Section 2058 of the California Masonic Code prevents wearing Masonic
clothing in public with three exceptions:
1. At the burial of a brother,
2. At the performance of some other strictly Masonic duty or ceremony, or
3. In accordance with the dispensation of the Grand Master.
The term "Masonic clothing" without doubt refers at least to white aprons
(see California Masonic Code 2788j, 2058b 2059, 2026c). Some of the same
authorities refer also to aprons of rank or office. No section refers to a hat or
officers' jewels.
The Master's hat and the officers' jewels are known by us to be a part of
proper Masonic attire. We know of no policy_ of the Grand Lodge that would
militate against including them as part of Masonic clothing. Therefore, the
Grand Master has authority to grant dispensation allowing wearing of station
aprons, officers' jewels, and Masters' toP. hats as part of Masonic cfothing and
regalia in public procession, meeting or places and the Grand Master's decision
1s correct.
The Policy and General Purposes Committee recommends a "Yes" vote.

The Committee on Ritual:
The Committee on Ritual concurs with the Policy Report and recommends
a "Yes" vote.
Decision APPROVED.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Section 1208 of the California Masonic Code requires approval of the Committee on Temple Properties before purchasing, encumbering or leasing
pro~rties for more than three years, ano before contracting for or commencmg the construction, alteration or improvement of a Masomc Temple ..."
The purpqse of this review is to assure financial respon,sibility before
pr~editig with certain kinds of work. This benefits both the Lodge ana Grand
Lodge.
The requirement of Committee review depends upon two things:
1.The kind of work. and
2.The am911nt tp be spent.
.
.
Before 1976) the amount to be spent without review could be up to
$2,500.00. In 1970, the amount was increased to $5,000.00.
As to the kind of work, as the Grand Master has pointed out, the languag_e
at one time was "to be erected or altered." In 19 , the language of the work
covered was modified to read "construction, alteration or improvement."
The addition of the word "improvement" must mean something. What it
means must be something other tfian construction and alteration. Those two
words could m-operly be construed as alteri~ or adding to the structural as~ct
of a Masonic"Temple only. The added word improvement" would not be added
if it meant the same thing.
As a practical matter the Section does not clearly deal with maintenance.
We think lhere was a reason for that. The reason is that fiscal responsibility is
required whether it be expensive construction, alteration or maintenance.
If a monetary limit is unrealistic because of inflation, we can increase that.
If there is a problem with slow Committee response, that can be dealt with.
In certain emerg~ncy situations, we do not doubf that the Grand Master can
give approval wilbout reference to the Temple Properties.

The Committee on Temple Properties:
In reviewing the Grand Master's Decision No. 3, we would like to remind
the Grand Lodge that the original name of the Committee on Temple Properties was the Loage Finance Committee, whose principal function was to try to
prevent Lodges or Temple Associations from spending beyond their means ;for
repairs and/or improvement o~ their Temples. We slilI regard this as a most important function of our Committee.
The approval of this Decision could, in some instances, result in a Temple
Association spending more than it could afford, or, in the case of a loan, be able
to repay.
Keeping a check on the financial status of a Temple Association by way of
the annual "Form 200" Profit and Loss and Financial Statements, and bemg able
lo determine how an Associatrion can and will _pay for improvements and alterations it plans to make is, in our opinion, far more important than subcategorizing the type of work lo be done.
H owever, disregarding those considerations, this Committee after hearing
the opinions ofbuikling contractors, architects and engineer5;,is of the opinion
that fhese specific cases e ntailing roof and gutter repairs anC11or replacement,
are de finitely not of a cosmetic nature, such as the replacement of a carpet, but
are necessary and structural by their very nature.
We therefore strongly recommend a "No" vote on the Grand Master's
Decisio n No. 3.
Decision APPROVED.

171e Committee on' Jun'sprudence:
Yo ur Committee on Jurisprudence, to which was referred the Grand

The Grand Master reported that at the 1987 Imperial Session the Ancient
Arabic Order Nobles of tile Mystic Shrine amended subsections (e) and (t) of
Section 323.8 of Article 23 of the by-laws of its Iowa corporation concerning
retention of membership. The amendment purportedly allows a member who
loses his membership in a prerequisite body lor any reason other than non-payment of dues to appeal to the Imperial Council for review. If the Imperial Council determines the reason for loss of membe rs hip in the prerequisite
o rganizatio n is not because of a violation of Shrine law, the member, although
susP.Cndcd or expelled from the prerequisite organization will nevertheless
retain membership in his Shrine Temple.
Grand Master Levitt promptly issued his Edict as repo rted in his Message
to the Grand Lodge.
A parallel (although not an identical) amendment to the same section of
Article 23 of the by-laws was enacted at the Imperial Session of the Shrine in
1978. The import of the Shrine legislative action in both 1978 and 1987 is,
however\ identical in permitting a man who has been suspended or expelled by
his constituent Lodge, and thus suspended or expelled from the bodies prereq-

Section 100 of the California Masonic Code stales:
"The Grand Lodge is the Supreme Masonic Power and Authority in this
Jurisdiction and is vested with all legislative, executive, and t"udicial powers1
limited onlY. by a strict adherence to tfle Ancient Landmarks o the Order, ana
by the provisions of it's own Constitution and R egulations."
Under Section 7 of the California Masonic Code:
"The jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge includes all Lodges and Masons
within the territorial limits of this state, all Lodges and their members without
this Stale, acting under it's authority, and mem5ers of Lodges of this Jurisdiction wherever residing."
The Judicial Powers of a constituent Lodge are defined in Section 2030 of
the California Masonic Code as follows:
"The Lodge shall exercise discipline over its own members (except the
Master), and all other Masons within its jurisdiction, except as such powers are
limitedoy the provisions of this Code regulating_ to penal 1urisdiction of lodges
under dispensation subject always to a revision-by {he Grand Lodge upon appeal."
Section 2032 of the California Masonic Code forbids any member of a constituent Lodge from holding Masonic intercourse with an expelled or suspended
Mason.
Under Section 2612 of the California Masonic Code:
"All members of organizations within the territorial jurisdiction of this
Grand Lodge, the prereq_uisite of membership wherein is that a person be a
Master Mason, shall be subject to the same standards of conduct and propriety
as are or may be imposed upon Master Masons in this jurisdiction."
Correlating these sections of the California Maso nic Code, your
Jurisprudence Committee makes these observations:
1.The Masonic legi~lative, executive and judicial powers of the Grand
Lodge are supreme in fhis Jurisdiction.
2.The standards of conduct and propriety imposed by the Grand Lodge
uwn Master Masons in this Jurisdiction extend to al l members of organizations
within the territorial jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge, the prerequisite of membership wherein is tliat a person be a Master Mason.
3.AH Master Masons within the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge arc forbidden from holding Masonic intercourse with an expelled or suspended
Mason.
4.When a Master Mason within the Jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge is expelled or susp_ended, all further Masonic intercourse with him is terminated and
he is denied the rights and privileges of a Master Mason. By such expulsion or
suspension, all Masonic intercourse is terminated whether it originates at the

"PUBLIC SCHOOLS -- CORNERSTONE OP ENLIGHTENMENT"

MASONI C HOMES ENDOWMENT MONTH

At the birth of our Nation over 200 year• ago, our Pounding Pathere faced
many problem•. Chief among these was a deep concern for the future of our
If our fledgling Republic waa to become a great Nation, i t was
Country.
clear that we must have an enlightened, well educated citizenry.

WHEREAS

Masonic traditions and c haritable o bligations have been
exemplified by o ur Masonic Homes, which have pro vided secu r i ty,
companionship and loving care for our elderly and love, educat i on
and stability to our deserving children; and

To achieve this goal our Pounders established a new system of education -a concept hitherto unknown in the world of their day -- a system of free
public education, thus creating the great Public School System we enj o y
today . The ensu ing year1 reveal that they acted wisely .

WHEREAS

Charity, in the Maso nic sense, means to relieve the wan ta a n d
distresses o f others, to assist a Brother, and raise t h e f allen,
and t h us to be charitable, o ne must have 4 sympatheti c understand i ng o f human pro b l ems and needs; and

Our Public Schools have
Today, we can look with pride on the result.
taught generations of America's youth to appreciate democracy and to value
their freedom; to attain proficiency in the vocation• and professions that
enhance our standard of living and to acquire the skill• of leadership
that have made our Country preeminent a1110ng world powers . Our PUBLIC
SCHOOLS are indeed the CORNERSTONE OP ENLIGHTENMENT.

WHEREAS

It is the observance of the v i rtue of char i ty that most n early
reveals mens' kinship to God, hence to contribut e to a nd s u ppo rt
our Masonic Homes is to pract i ce this v irtue, which will result in
a reci p r o city rich i n Broth erly love and sincere appreciat ion.

The schools could not have achieved these results had it not been for the
Inasmuch as such support is v i tal to
loyal support of a concerned public.
the well-being and effectiveness of our schools, i t is essential that i t
I therefore, call upon
be vigorously fostered and constantly maintained.
all citizens , especially my Brethren in Freemasonry, to continue their
support of this great Institution -- our Public Schools -- and do hereby
Procla i m
PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEX during April 1987
throughout California and Hawaii, and I call upon all Masonic Lodges to
arrange with the schools in their area for a mutually convenient week in
the Month of April to be set aside for appropriate ceremonies and program•
particularly aimed at the concept of PUBLIC SCHOOLS -- CORNERSTONE OP
ENLIGHTENMENT .
Furthermore, I direct that no Lodge programs or meetings, other than

NOW THEREFORE,

MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT MONTH

and urge each Maso n in Californ i a and Hawaii to lend financial suppo rt t o

UNFINISHED BUSINESS FROM 1986
PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO THE ORDINANCES

We do, however, in the absence of definitive guidelines, find several unanswered questions which may present themselves m the future. Some of which
are as follows:
1. In areas where there are many public and community organizations
would the Lodge be accused of preferential treatment where some could be
accommodatecf, while others coufd not?
2. Is it possible that these organizations might utilize this generous offer to
hold fund raising events to their own benefit?
3. Will there be sufficient safeguards to prevent these organizations from
carrying out some activity that is otherwise prohibited by Masonic law?
4. Is it indeed more Masonic to cater to these entities, and yet deny free
rent to affiliated Masonic organizationions in distress?
None of the problems that we have envisioned are insurmountable and are
reported at this time to suggest vigilance in future administration of the
program.
We recognize that many Lodges do not have the facilities or resources to
implement tli1s plan. We should not, however, restrict those Lodges that have
the means to be innovative and creative in projecting a strong Masonic image
in their community.
Your Policy and General Purposes Committee recommends a "Yes" vote
on Grand Master Driskell's Recommendation No. 1.

CHANGE OF NAME OF LODGE NO. 596
(87-1)
The proponents seek to change the name of Lodge No. 596 from "Guardian Jordan-Golden Bowl" to "Southeast".

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A .M. of California:
WHEREAS, Guardian Jordan-Golden Bowl Lodge No. 596 F. & A. M.,
respectfully requests that its name be changed; and
WHEREAS, the name Guardian Jordan-Golden Bowl Lodge is long and
unwieldy and difficult; and
WHEREAS, it would be difficult to select one of the above names over the
other; and
WHEREAS, the Lodge, at the December 1986 Stated Meeting, selected a
committee to present a new name for the consolidated Lodge; and
WHEREAS, the name selected by the committee was presented as a
Resolution at the February 1987 Stated Meeting in accordance with Sections
2022, 2082, and 2086, CMC., and every member was notified via United States
Mail of such Resolution, and the Resolution was ap{>roved by more than twothirds of the membership at the regular Stated Meeting of March 2, 1987.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the name of Guardian
Jordan- Golden Bowl Lodge No. 596 F. & A . M . be changed to:
SOUTHEAST LODGE NO. 596 F. & A. M.

OPEN CEREMO NIES· OPTIONAL USE
OF COLOR GUARD
(87-3)
The proponents of this Resolution seek to clarify who may act as a Color
Guard at Lodge Ceremonies which are open to the public.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS , this Grand Lodge is. a strong supporter and advocate of
patriotism to the United States of America; and
WHEREAS , an example of that patriotic spirit is the requir<:ment in Section 2060 of the California Masonic COde, that the Flag of the Umted States be
displayed at every meeting of a Lodge; and

194

PRECEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNlA

WHEREAS, the Flag is to be presented in proper form, and with proper
respect, at all official functions under the auspices of the Grand Lodge such as
Installati<?ns of Officers, the laying of Cornerstones, and Mortgage Burning
Ceremorues; and
. WHEREAS, it is desirable to encourage cooperation and close communication between Lodges and recognized Masonic-related organizations within
this Jurisdiction; and
WHEREAS, one means that such cooperation and communication could
be furthered would be by the use of Color Guards from Masonic-related organization to present the Flag at Lodge meetings or ceremonial functions which
are open to the public; and
WHEREAS, while there are specific guidelines in the Monitor and
Officers' Manual concerning the presentation of the Flag by the Marshal at tiled
!De~t~ngs of a Lodge, t~ere are no specific instructions or guidelines as to what
md1vtduals or groups, 1f any, other than the Marshal, are authorized to present
the Flag at Lodge meetings or ceremonial functions which are open to the
public, other than the suggestion that the Youth Groups may present the Flag
at Installations of Officers.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that in their arrangement for
and conduct of ceremonies which are open to the public, Lodges are encouia~ed, althou,lth not reguired, to invite one or more of the Masonic-related
orgaruzations in this Jurisdiction, including, but not limited to the Order of DeMolay, Order of Rainbow for Girls, Order of Job's Daughters, Knights
Templar, Order of the Eastern Star, and the Legion of Honor of the Shrine to
participate by providing a Color Guard for the Flag of the United States. S~ch
Color Guard shall be re~ponsi.ble for prest;nting the Flag at the ceremony in a
proper manner, complying with any requ1Tements of the Grand Lodge and
Government of the United States.

To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
Resolution.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Proponents of this Resolution seek to expand upon those who may act
as a Color Guard at Lodge ceremonies which are open to the public.
The Grand Lodge Policy and General Purposes Committee concurs with
th.e intent expressed by the proponents of this Resolution. Masons are patriotic
and long have espoused good government and love of country. Honor and
respect for our Flag is every Mason's duty; and the display of the Flag at Lodge
meetings, open or closed, should be encouraged.
Color guard of Masonic-related organizations, if properly attired and
smartly carrying out their duties when presentin~ the Flag of our country, could
add much to the solemnity, excitement, and enjoyment of any Lodge meeting
to which the public is invited; and the use of such Color Guards should be encouraged and lead to greater communication between Masonic Lodges and the
Masonic-related organizations involved.
This Resolution does not mandate any required action by the Lodge or its
Master, but only encourages the suggested action. The Master of a Lodge, undoubtedly, already has authority to do what is provided in this Resolution.
However, the suggestion when set out in print in the Masonic Code may
alert some Masters to the benefits to be obtained by inviting a Masonic related
organization Color Guard to participate in the Flag ceremonies at a meeting
which is open to the public. If so, it would be beneficial.
The Policy and General Purposes Committee, therefore, recommends a
"Yes" vote on this Resolution.

The Committee on Ritual:
Our monitor already provides when, how and who should present the Flag.
To comply with the intent of the resolution would necessitate the revision of all
our ceremonies. In the interest of harmony, our Installation Service provides
and is restricted to recognized youth groups presenting the Flag. The Committee on Ritual feels that any changes in our ceremonies would only complicate
these long established, traditional rituals.
The Committee on Ritual recommends a "No" vote.
Resolution ADOPTED.

PROFESSIONAL IN-DEPTH STUDY
(87-5)
The proponen t of this Resolution seeks to authorize the Executive Committee .and the Gran~ Secret~ !O contract wit~ a professionaJ, disinterested,
impartial non-Mas onic orgamzat10n to make an m-depth study and report concerning the "health" of Freemasonry in California and Hawaii.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

WHERE AS, a condition of poor health in California and Hawaiian
Freemaso nry has existed for some years about which Masons should not refer
to negatively, but about which thoughtful Masons should be seriously concerned; and
WHERE AS, statistical studies show as a partial basis for such concern that
between 1960 and 1986, inclusive, our Fraternity has suffered a net loss of 70,393
(29.31%) members, most of that loss occurring since 1965; that between 1960
and 1986, inclusive, 41,623 members were suspende d for N.P. dues -- reflecting
loss of interest; that between 1960 and 1986, of the 117,559 candidate s initiated,
only 105,829 became Master Masons; that the total of candidat es initiated in
1960 was 7,056 while in 1986 there were only 2,227; that deaths between 1960
and 1985 remain fairly constant between approximately 5,500 and 5,700 each
year; that the average age of our members steadily increases; that average annual Lodge dues in 1960 were $15.31 and in 1986 were only $30.10; that of 711
Lodges in existence in this Jurisdiction in 1965 there are now less than 600; and
WHERE AS, in the past many of our Masonic leaders during their terms
of office have suggested and prescribe d remedies for the illness which in their
best judgmen t would be cures, none has first found the basic ~of our poor
Masonic health. Most have pointed out results of our illness, but not the causes,
so the medications prescribe d have not been effective, and the losses and disinterest continue. Each thoughtful Mason has his own personal solutions for the
problems. Most are clouded by emotion or too close attachme nt to the Fraternity, which preclude s impartial and analytical judgmen ts; and
WHERE AS, it is believed that there continues to exist a pressing need to
clarify how our Masonic Fraternity fits in among today's overall cultural structure. and whether or not it is suffering from problems that may be currently endemic to all other structure d social organizations or from its own specialized
weaknesses; and
WHERE AS, it is believed further that the best method to determin e the
causes for our Fraternit y's problems is to employ a professional, disintere sted,
impartial non-Masonic organization to make an m-depth study and report, one
with adequate manpower which would be highly skilled in research coordina tion and anaJysis in matters of sociology, demography, psychology, public polls,

economics, and the relationship of these and similar elements to Masonry and
to the ~eneral public. For unless the causes of the plight of Freemasonry are
determmed, we cannot re-establish it as the respected, desirable, practical
spiritual, and socially beneficial organization it has been in the past; and
'
WHEREAS, in 1980, personal contact by the Grand Secretary was made
with such a professional organization and rough cost estimates for such study
and report were then $140,000.00 to $175,000.00, costs in 1988 would probably

PRECEEDINGS OF THE

Some of our critics, both in and out of the Fraternity, agree with this report.
Our good Brother, the Reverend George A. Burns, a member of Red Lion
Lodge No. 649 in Pennsylvania, responded to the critics and to the report as follows:
"Masonry, like the Bible, is filled with imagery, symbolism, parables, historical narratives and other literary forms. To mterpret any passage literally
when it is symbolic would distort the meaning, whether it be in the Bible or in
.
Masonic ritual."
He went on to say that "he could excuse the Bishops for their incorrect interpretation of Masonic ritual because they are not Masons. It is wrong,
however," he said, "to rush to change our Obligations to attempt to comply with
misguided criticism. Such a policy can only weaken our beloved Masonic Fraternity."
It is ironic that the Bishops should refer to the Bible, the same book that
lies open on our Masonic altar, in concluding their report. Let's take an example
from that source, using the "Sermon on the Mount" found in Matthew 5:29-30:
"And if thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out and cast it from thee; for it is
profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not thy whole
body. And if thy right hand offend thee, cut it off and cast it from thee; for it is
profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not thy whole
body."
It was not intended, as a condition of repentance, that we mutilate and
destroy ourselves. But if this passage was taken literally a good portion of our
population would be blind Jaraplegics. Shall we also consider the passage
regarding Christ as the brea of Life, found in John 6:56-57:
"He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, dwelleth in me, and I in
him. As the living Father has sent me, and I live by the Father, so he that eateth
me, even shall he live by me."
A literal interpretation of this passage could only lead to the conclusion
that it was proposing cannibalism. Actually it is intended to promote a relation.
ship with the Son analogous to the Son's relationship with the Father.
These are but two examples of man. They are used only as examples and
are not intended to express religious views or values.
My Brethren, if the Conference of Catholic Bishops, and others, can regard
the above mentioned passages from a figurative point of view, can't we, as
Masons, view our own ritual with the same generous and knowledgeable interpretation.?
We recommend and urge a "No" vote on Resolution Nos. 87-6 and 87-7.
The Committee on Ritual:
We regret that the proponents of this Resolution find certain portions of
the language of our ritual somewhat offensive. We have seen no harm come to
any member present or past because of current verbiage.
The Committee OD Ritual therefore recommends a "No" vote.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.

171e Committee on Finance:
Addressing the public speaking portion of the Resolution.
This Resolution calls fo r the Grand Lecturer, the Assistant Grand Lecturers, and the Inspectors lo instructt the Lodge Officers in the techniques of
public speaking. To do this, they will of course have to be trained public speakers
themselves. To insure that the Grand Lecturer, the Assistant Grand Lectureres,
and the Inspectors are current on the techniques necessary, they will have to go
to school.
Utili1ing the public schools, in the form of the California State College system and the California Community College system (and my apoligies to those
Lodges in Hawaii for not having figures for that State), the Committee has arrived at the following facts. Our State College system provides a course entitled
Communications 108 which takes two hours per night, two nights per week for
ten weeks. The cost of this course is $158.00 plus books and has a one time enrollment fee of $35.00. The Community College system provides a course entitled Speech 1 which takes three hours per night, one night per week, for
eighteen weeks and costs $15.00 plus books. Assuming that the Grand Lecturer,
the Assistant Grand Lectureres, and the Inspectors have the time available in
their already busy sched ules to take either of these courses, we then have the
following costs and related per capita tax. Please note that these figures include
tuition only. Using one Grand Lecturer, seven Assistant Grand Lecturers. and
one hundred twenty-five Inspectors for a total of one hundred thrity-three times
either the $15.00 for Community Colleges or the $193.00 for State Colle~es, we
arrive at a range of from $1,990.00 to $25,669.00 or $.01 to $.16 per capita. The
Finance Committee suggests that it may require several years to accomplish this
Resolution.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
There is no question our Lodges should cultivate interest and enthus~asm
in our Entered Apprentice and Fellowcraft Masons. However your Committee
on Policy and General Purposes believes there are already many avenues to involve them in our Lodge activities. Exampl~ are: .Public Schools and Constit.ution Observance Programs, Stated Meeting Dmners and all Lodge social
programs. In addition, since this is a learning period, too much emphasis cannot be placed in the areas on Candidate Coaching and Masonic Education.
Much of the incentive for candidate advancement lies in the desire to become a Master Mason, to possess all the secrets of Freemasonry and to have
the right to participate in all Lodge actrivitics. To admit Entered Apprentices
and Fellowcraft Masons into our Stated Meetings as observers, but not as participants, would remove some of the incentive while contributing little to the
candidate or the Lodge.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.

The Committee on Jurispmdence:
Your Committee on J urisprudcnce to which Resolutio n No. 87-19 has been
referred, reports as follows:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to amend Section 2048 of the
California Masonic Code by specifically authorizing Lake Tahoe Lodge No. 707
to meet in the place described in its Charter even though the building contains

a bar.
Your Committee finds that the legislation as distributed by the Grand
Secretary to the constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the intent of the
proponents.
This Resolution seeks to amend an Ordinance and a five-sixths affirmative
vote for adoption is required.
To place the matter before Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
Resolution.

The Committee 011 Policy 011d General Purposes:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposaes has given due consideration to Resolution No. 87-19 and to the persuasive arguments contained
therein relating to the problems experienced oy Lake Tahoe Lodge No. 707.
It is the opinion of this Committee that some changes to Section 2048 of the
California Masonic Code are inevitable. We do not, llowever, agree that they
should come in this form. If this amendment is adopted it is conceivable that a
myriad of arrangements, whether similar or not, would be forthcoming from
other Masonic and Masonic related organizations as the basis for appeal to circumvent the intent of Section 2048.
We find the Resolution to be improvident in that it fails to recognize any
other problems except those of Lake Tahoe Lodge No. 707.
This Committee has long been consistent in its opposition to issues that establish a _{>Olicy of single interest. We believe that exceptions to our law should
be admimstered to all Lodges on an equal basis. This should not be construed
as an endorsement of any proposed legislation written or unwritten.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.

The Committee on Jurisprndence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence to which Resolution No. 87-20 has been
referred, reports as follows:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to amend Sections 2048 and 2050
of the California Masonic Code so as to limit the restrictions imposed regarding alcoholic beverages to constituent Lodges only.
Your Committee finds that the legislation as distributed by the Grand
Secretary to the constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the intent of the
proponents.
This Resolution seeks to amend an Ordinance and a five-sixths affirmative
vote for adoption is required.
To place the matter before Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
resolution.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Proponents of this Resolution claim that Sections 2048 and 2050 of the
California Masonic Code cause disharmony, are ineffective, are a problem for
Grand Lodge delegates and Concordant Bodies and pit Brother against
Brother. They propose to solve these problems by relieVIng the Concordant
Bodies of any responsibility to comply with these Regulations.
The J?rohibition against the use of alcoholic beverages has been a part of
Masonry m California since Lodges were first chartered in the gold rush days.
The regulations were easy to understand and simple to enforce because there
were no exceptions.
In 1966 and 1969 Grand Lodge approved chan~es which liberalized the
restrictions on alcoholic beverages as regards meetmg place limitations and
serving liquor at social functions. These are the actions which created Sections
2048 and 2050 and also caused the problems and confusion to which the
proponents refer.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes agrees that there may be
problems with these two Sections that need to be dealt with. However, if any
changes are contemplated by this Grand Lodge, they should not exclude the
Masonic Lodges and disregard what might be in their best interests. Any
benefits derived from modifying or deleting these Sections should apply equally to the Lodges and the Concordant Bodies.
For the above reasons, your Committee on Policy and General Purposes
strongly recommends a "No" vote.

The Committee on Taxation:
Resolutions Nos. 87-20, 87-21, 87-22, 87-23, 87-24,87-25, 87-26, 87-28, 8729 and 87-31 have been referred to your Committee on Taxation to comment
on the possible tax consequences of each of them. To understand the possible
tax consequences, it is important to understand how Masonic Lodges are taxed.
Masonic Lodges are exempt from all Fe.deral and California income taxes,
regardless of the amount of income from dues, interest, dividends or income
from other investments, with certain exceptions. A Lodge is taxed on income
from a trade or business which is unrelated to the fraternal purposes of the

218

PRECEEDING S OF THE

Lodge. When exempt organizations, such as Masonic Lodges, compete with taxpaying businesses, the. income from that competitive actiVIty is taxed to remove
any economic advantage which exempt status might have conferred. This income is known as "unrelated business income". For example, net income from
a working oil interest would be taxable because such an interest is considered
a trade or business.
To constitute a trade or business, however, the activity must be regularly
carried on. This does not include periodic events. Operating a restaurant constitutes a trade or business. H olding periodic dinners does not constitute a trade
or business. In addition, income from events conducted by tax-exempt fraternal organizations, such as Masonic Lodges, are not taxable if substantially all of
the labor required to hold the event is performed for the Lodge without compensation.
There arc also potential California sales and use tax consequences to certain Lodge events. A sales tax is assessed upon the sale of tangible personal
property. The sale of tangible personal property includes furnishing meals as
well as supplying merchandise al garage sales or bazaars for a purchase price,
even if the purchase price is labeled as "donation".
There is one exemption to the sales and use tax available to Lodges,
however. Social clubs and fraternal organizations, such as Masonic Lodges, are
not subject to the sales tax on their receipts from furnishing meals if the meals
are furnished exclusively to members and are furnished less frequently than
once a week .Both these requirements must be met. If the Lodge furnishes meals
to non-members, all receipts from meals are subject to tax, whether the meals
are furnished lo members or non-members. However, meals paid for by members are considered furnished to the members and are therefore not subject to
the sales tax even though consumed by guests who are not members. Thus, tickets for non-members who attend Lodge dinners should be purchased by members of the Lodge. The Lodge need not thereafter concern itself with whether
the member obtains any reimbursement from the guest.
Any other transfers of tangible personal property by the Lodge, such as at
garage sales or bazaars, are subject to the sales tax. If the Lodge is subject to
the sales tax, it must apply for a California Seller's permit. These can be obtained from the local office of the State Board of Equalization.
These unrelated business income tax and sales and use tax rules apply to
Masonic Temple Associations also.
Because Resolution No. 87-20 does not propose to permit a Masonic Lodge
or Temple Association to sell or serve alcoholic beverages, the adoption of tliis
Resolution would have no tax consequences to them.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 87-21 proposes to exempt the Shrine from the provisions of
Sections 2048, 2050 and 3314 of the California Masonic Code. It is, by its very
nature, a gross example of single interest legislation.
The policy position of this Committee has been previously stated regarding the adoption of issues that do not give equal consideration to all organizations of equal standing.
We reco~nize the impact that the Shrine has made upon our society, but,
other Masonic related organizations have, to the extent of their ability, made
contributions in the name of Freemasonry. It would be most unfair to single out
any concordant or appendant body as the beneficiary of special legislation.
There are more comprehensive Resolutions on today's agenda for your
consideration, dealing in part with this subject, however Resolution No. 87-21
should be rejected on its own merit.

171e Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has, during the term of
this Grand Lodge year, been used as a sounding board by many members of this
Grand Jurisdiction on matters which they believed to be of paramount importance to the. future of Craft Masonry in California and Hawaii. Without a doubt
the subject of meeting places and related activities therein has been the most
prominent.
This Committee, as a matter of policy, has long been opposed to any form
of change to our regulations governing the use of alcoholic beverages in the
meeting places of Masonic and Masonic related organizations. Such a policy
was, in the opinion of the Committee, in the best interests of our fraternal image.
It is possible that we erred in our judgment.
Resolution No. 87-23 is consistent with our approach to legislative change
in that it gives equal consideration to all Masonic entities including the several
Lodg.es of this Jurisdiction. In it also are safeguards against the intrusion of alcohol into any and all meeaings of a business nature.We believe further that
should any serious breach of Masonic standards occur under this amendment,
if adopted, it is well within the conscience of this Grand Lodge to make any
technical adjustments in the future to make it workable.
My Brethren, in summary, the message this Committee has received from
you is, that you want some reform to our laws; that the "gold rush" days are over
and we can, as Lodges, conduct ourselves agreeably to society's highest stan.dards; that you want equal application of the law to all segments of our Masonic
family; that you want the law to be clear, complete and concise. We believe
Resolution No. 87-23 to be the best proposal before us in addressing this "shopping list" of issues.
We recommend a "Yes" vote.
17ie Committee on Taxation:

Your Committee on Taxation has been asked to comment on the possible
tax consequences of this Resolution. The general tax consequences of Masonic
Lodge and Temple Association events and sales were discussed in our report
on Resolution No. 87-20.
The adoption of Resolution No. 87-23 would permit Masonic Lodges and
Temple Associations to sell alcoholic beverages. For the reasons discussed in
our report on Resolution No. 87-20, the sale of alcoholic beverages could result
in income tax liabaility unless alcoholic beverages are never sold but given away,
are sold infrequently or are only sold at events where substantially all the labor
required to hold the event is performed without compensation. The sale of alcoholic beverages would likely be subject to sales tax.
(See Resolution No. 87-20 for the Insurance Committee report.)

Your Committee on Jurisprudence to which Resolution No. 87-24 has been

The proponents of this Resolution seek to repeal Sections 2048, 2050 and

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The preamble to the Resolution No. 87-24 presents an abstract lesson in
Constitubonal Government and Law which was interesting, but, not germane
to the issue at hand. This same Constitution which, by amendment, permits the
sale, manufacture and transportation of intoxicating liquors within the several
states also permits, within the framework of states rights, gambling, prostitution, abortton clinics and uncelibate activities in singleness. Such permissive
rights by Constitutional Government do not furnish compelling reasons for our
Fraternity to consider any or all of these activities as a part of our Masonic agenda.
As an integral part of "We The People" we have the right to set our own
standards of conduct and morality. Thus, your Committee on Policy and
General Purposes will view Resolutton No. 87-24 on its fraternal merits alone.
We have heard, as you have, the comments from up and down this state
calling for some reform, or so called "middle ground", in our regulations governing meeting places and the permitted activities therein. Resolution No. 87-24
completely ignores that "middle ground". If our laws, as they are written, are extremely restrictive, then, this Resolution would be equally permissive to the extreme.
The deletion of Sections 2048, 2050 and 2314, without substitute legislation,
would completely ignore some of the basic reasons for the adoption of these
regulations in the first place. Almost all of our laws represent a reaction, by the
collective body of California and Hawaii Freemasonry, to an action of some
Lodge, Lodges or individual Masons who could not ably regulate, control and
supervise the mission of Masonry in their trust.

To place the matter before Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
One of the more common complaints about Section 2048 and 2050, aside
from the restrictions, is that they are difficult to understand, interpret and enforce.
The proponents of this Resolution seek to amend these two Sections to
remove virtually all of the restrictions against the use of alcoholic beverages in
the banquet rooms of Masonic Temples, at Masonic socials and non-Masonic
functions. In fact, to accomplish this, they have virtually re-written the two Sections and appear, if anything, lo have made them more complex, and in some
instances, difficult, if not impossible to enforce.

Examples of some of the problem areas are:
(1) The provisions for leasing to a liquor store or establishment;
(2) Definition of the term "undesirable for use";
(3) Definition of Masonic and non-Masonic purpose;
( 4) Definition of Masonic and non-Masonic organization;
(5) Enforceme.nt of compliance with all laws, rules and regulations
regarding the serving or dispensing of alcoholic beverages;
(6) Enforcement of requirement for obtaining all required Governmentaf permits.
Resolution No. 87-23 is more easily understood and therefore, more appropriate.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.

171e Committee on Taxation:
Your Committee on Taxation has been asked to comment on the possible
tax consequences of this Resolution. The general tax consequences of Masonic
Lodge and Temple Association events and sales were discussed in our report
on Resolution No. 87-20.
The ado ption of Resolution No. 87-25 would permit Masonic Lodges and
Temple Associations to sell alcoholic beverages. For the reasons discussed in
our report on Resolution No. 87-20, the sale of alcoholic beverages could result
in income tax liability unless alcoholic beverages are never sold but given away,
are sold infrequently or are only sold at events where substantially all the labor
required to hold the event is performed without compensation. The sale of alcoholic bevrerages would likely be subject to sales tax.
(See Resolution No. 87-20 for Insurance Committee report.)
