Your Committee on Jurisprudenc e, to which R esolution No. 87-28 bas been
referred, reports as follows:

PRECEEDING S OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The proponents of this Resolution seek to amend the California Masonic
Code to provide that constituent Lodges and appendant bodies may invite the
general public to attend certain events sponsored by said Masonic and affiliated
groups, with the proceeds from fund raising events first going to the organization, and to the extent funds are not needed, then lo a charity of the Fraternity.
Your Committee finds that the legislation as distributed by the Grand
Secretary to the constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the intent of the
proponents.
The Resolution seeks to amend the Ordinances and requires a five-sixths
affirmative vote for adoption.
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
ResolutJon.

Our Lodges and Temples are not for the hustle and bustle of the commercial world. They are for the speculative work that we do. Hence, they should be
set apart and not used for commercial ventures.
The Committee on Commercialism recommends a "No" vote.
(See Resolution No. 87-20 for Insurance Committee report.)

236

The Committee on Policy a11d General Purposes:
The Proponents seek to amend, liberalize and remove current restrictions
from the California Masonic Code to allow Masonic Lodges and appendant
bodies to invite the public and solicit their financial support, similar to the (attitude allowed our Masonic Youth Groups.
This Resolution is cumbersome and very hard to follow with numerous ambiguities in the proposed changes. Its 100 words sentences make it impossible
to have two Masons read it with the same interpretation. If this Resolution were
approved, it would remove the current restrictions on fund raising and allow
wide open solicitation of the public.
Perhaps some of the commercialism rules should be changed in our California M asomc Code,but any changes should be written in layman's language which
are easily understood by the membership. With respect to Commercialism, we
believe that Resolution No. 87-29 is a better approach. We therefore, recommend a "No" vote on No. 87-28.

17ie Committee on Taxatio11:
Your Committee on Taxation has been asked to comment on the possible
tax consequences of this Resolution. The general tax consequences of Masonic
Lodge and Temple Association events and sales were discussed in our report
on Resolution No. 87-20.
The adoption of Resolution No. 87-28 would remove restrictio ns on
Masonic Lodges and Temple Associations holding fund-raising events to which
the public is invited. For the reasons discussed in our reP.?rl on Resolution No.
87-20, any profit earned could result in income tax liability unless such events
are held infrequently or substantially all the labor required to hold such events
is performed without compensation. The sale of tangible personal property at
such events could be subject to sales tax.

171e Committee on Commercialism:
This measure seeks to permit Lodges and other Masonic organizations to
hold social events on any calendar day and solicit the public to attend. This
coupled with the new Section 2069 gives the Craft a reasonable assurance that
these events will be properly conducted. This part of the measure is reasonable
and in line with the present custom.
This measure also wants our Lodges, or Temple Properties, to be allowed
to hold rummage sales or other commercial ventures to which the public support is solicited.

PUBLIC SUPPORT - FUND-RAISING EVENTS
(87-29)
The proponents of this Resolution seek to amend our Regulations to conform to what they stale to be the prior practices of many Masonic organizations
by permitting the sale of tickets to fund-raising events to family and friends.
To tile Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of Califomia:
WHEREAS, many Masonic Lodges, Eastern Star Chapters and other
Masonic organizations have for years sold breakfast, dinner and similar tickets

The Committee on Jurispntdence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which Resolution No. 87-29 has been
referred, reports as follows:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to amend our Regulations to conform to what they state to be the prior practice of many Masonic organizations
by permitting the sale of tickets to their fund-raising events to family and friends.
Your Committee finds that the legislation as distributed by the Grand
Secretary to the constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the intent of the
proponents.
As this Resolution does not amend the Constitution or Ordinances, a
simple majority is sufficient for adoption.
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
Resolution.
171e Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Many Lodges, Temple Associations, and other Masonic organizations,
have held breakfasts, dinners, card parties, dances, bazaars and so forth for the
purpose of making a profit to supplement the sponsoring Masonic
organization's annual budget. These events have been supported by the members, their families and friends.
Some have said that our rules do not permit this. If they do not, they should.
If your Lodge wants to hold a dinner or breakfast, sell tickets to family and
friends and earn a profit for the Lodge, we believe that our rules should permit
it. This Resolution would allow it.
We therefore, recommend a "Yes" vote.
17ire Committee on Taxation:

tax consequences of this Resolution. The general tax consequences of Masonic
Lodge and Temple Association events and sales were discussed in our report
on Resolution No. 87-20.

fund-raising events described in Article II of the Regulations Governing Organizations Subject to the Jurisdiction of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge,
F. & A. M. of California relating to public support could result in income tax
liability unless such events arc held infrequently or suhstantially all the labor re-

be sent to members who are in arrears in the payment of dues in excess of one
year; and
WHEREAS, it is considered, that the average yearly dues of Lodges range
from $25.00 to $35.00. The annual dues twenty years ago are estimatea to have
been in a range from $15.00 to $20.00. Statistical and economic calculations,
equating 1987 Dollars to 1967 Dollars are such, that the current dues of Lodges
represent a lesser percentage of individual spending income, than did the 1967
Dollar. Therefore, the need to pay dues quarterly has been substantially
eliminated, an.d must be considered to be no longer justified.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which Resolution No. 87-34 has been
referred, reports as follows:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to have the California Masonic
Code changed so that a Master Mason can vouch for a Brother if they have sat
together in a Tiled meeting of a recognized concordant body.
Your Committee finds that the legislation as distributed by the Grand
Secretary to the constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the mtent of the
proponents.
This Resolution seeks to amend an Ordinance and a five-sixths affirmative
vote for adoption is required.
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
Resolutton.
The Committee on Ritual:
Our Grand Lodge recognizes only the Entered Apprentice, Fellow Craft,
and Master Mason Degrees. It is the duty of the exanuning committee only to
ascertain whether or not an individual is a member.
To vouch for someone as a result of having sat with him in a concordant
body does not meet the criteria as to determining his being a Master Mason.
The Committee on Ritual recommends a "No" vote.

This Resolution seeks to amend Ordinances and a five-sixths affirmative
vote is required for adoption.
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
Resolution.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Under the present system of balloting on Applications, if one cube appears,
the Master, without declaring the result, orders a second ballot to correct a possible mistake. If two or more cubes appear, the Master declares the Applicant
to have been rejected.
The proponents of this Resolution seek to have a second ballot regardless
of how many cubes appear the first time. If the result is the same on the second
ballot, the Application would then be referred to a further investigating committee. If this investigating committee reports favorably, the Application will be
balloted upon again. This process will continue until no cubes appe.ar or until
an objection to the Applicant is made to the Master.
Applicants for our degrees must be elected by unanimous ballot and any
member of the Lodge has the right to vote for rejection with complete
anonymity. Certainly, we hope that tlie reasons for voting for rejection are truly
Masonic and in the member's sincere belief that it is in the best interests of the
Lodge. We also recognize that sometimes Applicants might be unfairly rejected
for reasons which are purely personal and have nothing to do with the welfare
of Masonry or of the particualar Lodge.
The rejection of an Applicant is always disappointing and frustrating, and
sometimes unfair. However, this proposal which seeks to force a member to
state his objection to an investigatmg committee or to the Master would render
the balloting process un-workable and would deny the right of anonymity to all
of our members. It could also result in the acceptance of Applicants who are
not worthy of membership in our Craft.
Your Committee on Policy and Gener al Purposes recommends a "No" vote.
The Committee on Ritual:
Masonry supports the many freedoms we enjoy in our country. One of these
freedoms is the right to vote. The right to vote is a.n obligation encumbent on all
citizens - so it is at our Stated Meetings. All members of the Lodge present must
vote. A member approaching the Altar and casting his ballot has the right to a
secret ballot.
Our Fraternity has always allowed one objection to reject an applicant, and
has always expected each member to put personal differences aside and ballot
honorably. The balloter, therefore, bas the right to expect his first ballot to be
respected and not have to re-ballot indefinitely.
The Committee on Ritual recommends a "No" vote.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of Resolution No. 87-38 propose to reduce the requirements for bemg proficient in the three degrees to knowing and understanding
the obligations and modes of recognition plus the apron lecture in the First
Degree. This Resolution poses two fondamental questions. Does this Grand
Lodge have the power to make the requested change? If it has the power, is this
an appropriate change to be made?
Under Section 2690 of the California Masonic Code, the Grand Lodge
alone has the power to authorize any changes in the ritual of the Order but then
only for the exclusive purpose of having the ritual remain as it was handed down
from time immemorial. Are the questions and answers of our proficiencies part
of our "ritual"? In the view of this Committee, they are. The ~uestions and
answers of our proficiencies are substantially similar to the catechisms found in
the lectures of the three degrees in England several centuries ago. These questions and answers arc established ceremonial forms of our Order performed at
regular intervals. Therefore, these questions and answers should be considerctd
part of our ritual.
However, the proponents of this Resolution do not seek to change the questions and answers. They seek only to reduce the number of answers to questions
which a candidate must answer m order to evidence his proficiency for advancement. Is it part of our ritual to require a candidate to memorize all of these
answers to evidence his proficiency? We have evidence that our English
brethren of several centurie.s ago who used substantially similar questions and
answers in their lectures to the candidates did not require their candidates to
memorize the entire set of answers in order to advance. Nowhere does our ritual
explain what is the necessary proficiency in the preceding degree required for
advancement. Many recognized Masonic jurisdictions elsewhere in the world
today use the answers to a dozen or so questions to test proficiency and do not
even require the candidate to memorize the obligation.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes is not the recognized
authority of this Grand Lodge on ritual but it does seem to the members of this
Committee that a candidate may make the required proficiency for advancement by learning fewer than all of the answers taught in our standard form of
proficiency and that such a reduced requirement should not be considered a
change in the ritual.
This brings us to our second question: is this proposal to reduce the length
of our proficiency an appropriate change? In the view of the Committee, it is
not. We share the concern of the proponents of the Resolution who recognize
that many candidates are now suspended for failure to advance and that this
failure may be due in part to the length and method of teaching our proficiencies. However, in our view, it would not constitute a satisfactory proficiency
merely to learn the obligations and modes of recognition plus the apron lecture
in the First Degree. In order to advance, a candidate must be proficient in that
which is the essence of Freemasonry. The essence of Freemasonry is not contained in the obligations alone but in the legend of the Third Degree, the principle tenets of the Order, the method of being made a Mason and the modes of

253

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes therefore recommends
a "No" vote.
17te Committee on Ritual:

S~atistics disclose t~at between 1960 and 1985, approximately 10% of those
applymg for membership in our Fraternity do not advance to the degree of
Master ~ason. We must assume that some of these losses are due to the difficulty wt th the profi<;ienq requirements. While the Committee on Ritual would
not have draft~d legislation exactly as that proposed, we agree with the intent
of the Resolution and recommend a "Yes" vote.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on J urispurdence, to which Resolution No. 87-42 has been
referred, reports as follows:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to allow a candidate to select the
Holy Wntings of his choice/belief on which to be obligated.
Your Committee finds that the legislation as distributed by the Grand
Secretary to the constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the intent of the
proponents.
This Resolution seeks to amend an Ordinance and a five-sixths affirmative
vote for adoption is required.
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
Resolution.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to allow a candidate to select the
Holy Wntings of his choice/belief on which to be obligated.
The purpose of any obligation is to impress upon the individual taking the
obligation the seriousness and the solemnity of the undertaking he is about to
agree to and enter into. Christians and Jews alike for many years, when being
obligated, have done so by placing their hand upon the Holy Bible. However,
the Bible is not the only Holy Writing. There are other faiths besides Christianity
and Judaism, and those other faiths, also, have their Holy Writings.
Masonry does not require a man to have or believe in a particular religion.
Masonry only requires that a man believe in a Supreme Being, a diety which
may be known by different names, depending on what part of the world and
what customs, culture, or religion is involved.
As Masonry makes no distinction between race, creed, or religion, and requires only that a candidate for the degrees of Free Masonry believe in God
and come well recommended under the tongue of eood report, the candidate
should be allowed to select the Holy Writings of his choice upon which to be
obligated, and those writings should be those which he most reveres, believes
and respects, in order to most impress upon him the importance of the degree
and the solemnity of the occasion.
Last year this Committee opposed a similar Resolution. This year, we support it. Io the intervening twelve months, members of this Committee have
reflected on the concerns raised on behalf of those who arc not Christians or
Jews, a~d believe that it is appropriate to address them as proposed by this
Resolution.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

257

The Policy and General Purposes Committee, therefore, recommends a
.Yes" vote.

The Committee on Ritual:
At the Annual Communication of 1976 this Grand Lodge adopted the
Recommendation of John F. Roberts, Jr. to form a Committee consisting of the
policy and General Purposes, Jurisprudence and Ritual Committees. The sole
purpose of this Committee was to determine what changes would be required
to permit an obligation to be taken on Holy Writings other than the Holy Bible.
That Committee reported as follows: "Jn making this study many factors
were considered by the Committee, each having a strong bearing upon the subject. The most important of these considerations, however, is the great number
of changes in our law and ritual, and additional problems for Lodges which
would result from the substitution of another book for the Holy Bible.
"Because of the complex nature of the study, the Committee deemed it advisable and necessary to seek additional advice of those more expert in the field
of Theology and Holy Writings. Opinions were therefore solicited from
Brothers Roland A. Bach and Rabbi Edgar Magnin, both former Grand
Chaplains and recognized authorities in the field of Theology.
"Both of these former Grand Chaplains stated that in their opinion, the
practice of substituting other books for the Holy Bible in obligating a Candidate
could lead to a myriad of problems. Both advised al?ainst instituting such a practice. To substitute another book for the Holy Bible m our dewees would require
substantive changes in our law to permit the necessary revisions to the adopted
California ritual. A change such as this could well lead to further, undesirable
changes in our present system of ritual. The problems which would be encountered would far outweigh any possible advantage to the Craft, or to any individual."
It was the reco}11mendation of that committee that the Holy Bible continue
to be the only book upon which all Candidates are obligated, bearing fully in
mind that the use of the Holy Bible in our degrees does not in any way imply
that Freemasonry is limited to a Christian belief. The findings of that Committee as reported here in 1977 are as valid today as then.
Your Committee on Ritual respectfully recommends a "No" vote.
Resolution HELD OVER.

PRECEEDINGS OF THE

It is a long established policy of this Grand Lodge that the Lodges should
arrange their financial affairs so that they may operate on a fiscally sound basis.
While the members of your Committee on Policy and General Purposes are not
actuarial experts, it docs not seem to us that the basis on which the Lodge membership fee is computed under the proponent's plan is actuarially and therefore
fiscally sound. Masons younger than age thirty-six would pay more under the
proponent's plan. But, most Masons are thirty-six and older and would pay less
than under our present plan. We believe that LodJ_;es would receive far less
monies under this Life Membership program than 1s provided by our present
program. This does not appear to be actuarially and therefore fiscally sound to
your Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
The proponent of the Resolution also seeks to establish a centralized fund
administered by the Grand Lodge for all Life Membership funds. We know of
no problems which the Lodges now have administering their own Life Membership funds which would be corrected by requiring them to transfer these
funds lo the Grand Lodge. Indeed, this would create additional administrative
cost in the Grand Lodge office which necessarily must be passed on to the membership either through an increased per capita tax or through a charf?e against
the earnings on the Life Membership funds before their income is distributed
to the Lodges. We see no reason to mcur this additional burden when we find
no problems which a centrally administered fund would resolve.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes therefore recommends
a "No" vote.

The Committee 011 Fina11ce:
The Grand Lodge Committee on Finance has analyzed the fiscal impact of
Resolution No. 87-44, which provides for the Grand Lodge to establish a Life
Membership Plan. This Plan to be administered by a special Grand Lodge Committee, with expert council of professional advisors, and that this Life Membership Plan may be purchased on a declining scale based on age of purchaser.
Taking into account the cost, for an employee to administer this Life Membership Plan, employee benefits, and an additional Committee expense the
Finance Committee estimates an additional per capita of $.15 be necessary if
this Resolution is adopted.
The Finance Committee docs no t offer a recommendation on this Resolution.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.

COST OF PURCHASE - LIFE MEMBERSHIP
(87-45)
The proponents of this Resolution seek to change Section 2804 of the
California Masonic Code regarding the cost of Life Memberships.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the determination of the cost of a Life Membership being related to the annual dues discriminates against a Lodge with small cash assets
and high annual dues compared to those with large cash assets and low annual
dues. The Life Membership fee for the small Lodges with high annual dues

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

261

revents the Lodge from obtaining Life Members thereby making it more difGcult to increase their cash assets and using interest to defray current expenses.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 2804 of the
California Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:
"2804. LIFE MEMBERSHIP. A Lodge may adopt a Standing Resolution
providing for a system of Life Membership, whiell shall forever exempt a
member Trom the pa~ent of dues therein. Said resolution or anY. amendment thereto shalf not be acted upon at the Stated Meeting at which it is
introduced, nor until notice in writing thereof shall have been forwarded
by mail to every member of the Lodge. It must provide that a Life Membership shall ~ _filanted upon payment of a minimufl! of $500.00 al age ~1
reduced by $5.00 for every year over the age of 21 at time of pa~ent. Said
Resolution shall take effect only upon its approval by the Grand Master."

The Committee on Jun'spntde11ce:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which Resolution No. 87-45 has been

referred, reports as follows:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to change Section 2804 of the
California Masonic Code regarding the cost of Life Memberships.
Your Committee finds that the legislation as distributed by the Grand
Secretary to the constituent Lodges is adequate to .carry out the mtcnt of the
•
proponents.
This Resolution seeks to amend an Ordinance and a five-sixths affirmative
vote for adoption is required.
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
Resolution.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to change Section 2804 of the
California Masonic Code regarding the cost of Life Memberships.
Specifically, this Resolution would provide for a minimum Life Membership fee of $500 to be paid by a mem~cr age 21, said fee to be ~educed by $5 for
every year over the age of 21 al the time of payment. The maximum fee is set at
$500 with no tie to the annual dues structure of the Lodge.
This Committee views the general concert of Life Membership with favor
as one of the potential solutions to the financia problems of many of our Lodges.
The poten.tial benefit, however, is a long-range one for any Lodge, that of the
Life Membership fees remaining with the Lodge, even after the death of the
member, to become a part of a permanent fund, the earnings from which could
help supply the current operating fund of the Lodge each year.
The proponents seek to favor Lodges with small cash assets and high annual dues. It would appear this Resolution, while it might have long range

262

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORN IA

PRECEEDI NGS OF THE

benefits to such Lodges, might, on the other hand, be detrimental to such
Lodges in the near term.
The current minimum Life Membership fee is a function of the annual dues
of the Lodge in such a way that the Life Membership fee needs to attain an investment return of only about 5% to supply the current operatin~ fund of the
Lodge with an amount equal to the sum the member would otherwise have paid
toward each year's current operating budget.
Under this Resolution, as an example, a 60-year old member of a Lodge
with annual dues of $40 (slightly higher than the $31 average of our Lodges)
could take out Life Membership for S305. That sum, in turn, would have to earn
13.11% or more in each and every year thereafter to SU{'plythe Lodge's current
operating budget with the same $40 it would have enjoyed from the member
had he not taken out Life Membership , ignoring any potential rise in annual
dues in the future. If, on the other hand, the Life Membership fund earned only
8% in any one year, the current operating budget of the Lodge would suffer by
some 39% for each member who took Life Membership at age 60. The numbers look worse as members wait later in life to take Life Membership . A male,
age 60 in this country has a life expectancey of some 17.4 years.
It would appear the declining schedule of Life Membership fees under this
Resolution would tend to encourage members to wait later in life to take Life
Membership since it would be less expensive for them for each year of advancing age and that the whole scheme would have a negative effect on the nearterm finances of the Lodge.
While we favor the concept of Life Membership , we are concerned about
the effect this Resolution would have on it and your Committee on Policy and
General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.

(87-47)
The proponents of this Resolution seek to give Lodges the option of notifying either Masonic Service Bureau or nearby Lodges of applications for the
degrees instead of only the latter as now required, and to have such notification
include applications for affiliation.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, Masonic Service Bureaus are required by Section 2904 of the
California Masonic Code to operate as clearing houses as to applicants for the
degrees of Lodges in the areas of such Bureaus; and
WHEREAS, the California Masonic Code makes no mention in this regard
of applicants for dual or plural membership by affiliation; and
WHEREAS, individual Lodges are required by Section 2618 of the California Masonic Code, within ten days after receipt, to notify other Lodges within
ten miles of their places of meeting of any applications they may receive for
degrees; and
WHEREAS, nowhere in the California Masonic Code are individual
Lodges required to furnish information regarding applications to Masonic Service Bureaus to enable such Bureaus to operate as clearing houses as they are
required to do by the Code; and
WHEREAS, the parentheses and numeral 10 contained therein are redundant and unnecessary in this modern day of typewriters and computers and are
no longer needed for avoiding confusion.
NOW, THEREFORE , BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 2618 of the
California Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:

"2618. JURISDICTIO N TO RECEIVE APPLICATIONS. Any Lodge of
this Grand Jurisdiction may receive and act on an application for any unconferred degree or degrees of Masonry from a qualified resident of this
Grand Jurisdiction. If the applicant is a candidate of another Lodge, his
apP.lication to be received must be accomP.anied bY. a release or wruver of
Jurisdiction from the Lodge of which he is a canaidate, directed to the
Lodge to which he is applymg.
"Within ten days after receiP.t of the application, a Lodge shall notify any
other Lodge or Lodges witliin ten miles of its place of meeting of any applications 1t maY. re.ceive for degrees or affiliation. Notification to the
Masonic Service Bureau in the area in which the Lodge is situated shall be
deemed to constitute notification to other Lodges wifhin ten miles."

To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

We view this Resolution primarily as a housekeeping one as it would
provide in the Lodge for practices which have been long established and practiced in this Jurisdiction.
It would seem the function of acting as a "clearing house" for Applications
for Degrees and for Affiliation would be a natural one for Masomc Service
Bureaus and fit comfortably into this operation.
On the other hand, whether there is a Masonic Service Bureau in an area
or not, if the Lod$es act as their own clearing house by the notification of each
other of Applications for Degrees and Affiliation, the need is served.
It should be noted there is nothing in this Resolution which would compel
a Lodge to join a Masonic Service Bureau in an area if it choses not to.
Your Committe e on Policy and General Purposes recommen ds a "Yes"
vote.

In order for the FraterniD> to hold a fund raising event to which the public
is invited, the following must be done:
Request permission from the Grand Master to hold the event. This should
be done, in writing, six to nine months in advance of the event. In your reuest one should provide the date, name and place of the event. Also tne group
ftoldfug thy event, along with the person in cbarge and the charity the profifs
are to oc given to.
Since the public is involved, the following rules will have to be adhered to:
1. All the net proceeds derived from the event (entire proceeds less
necessary expenses) are to be given to charity.
2. No division of the proceeds are to be made with any institution,
organizations group or individual other than the
pa~ent of necessary expenses.
3. No division of the P.roceeds are to be P.aid to any body of the
Fraternity or any of its concordant booies or suodivis10n
thereof for any of its activities.
4. A certified ana detailed accounting of all income and expenses are
to be prepared by a Certified Public Accountant within 60 days after
the event. The accountant's report along_ with documentation of the
Raying over of the net profits to the chanty are to be presented to
the Grand Lodge.
Should the public support not be requested, solicited or received, the following must be done:
Request permission from the Grand Master to hold the event. This should
be done in wnting, six to nine months in advance of the event. In your request,
one should provide the date, name and place of the event; also, the group holding the event, along ~th the person in charge and the name of the orgaruzation
the profits are to oe given to.
1. No advertising of the event be made by way of P,rint, electronic
or other medmm, publication, flyers, l:iumper stickers, posters,
bill-boards or notices of any nature; and
2. Notices and information of the event be given only to members
of the Masonic Fraternity holding the event; and

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of Ca/ifornia:

REPORT OF THE INVESTMENT COMMITTEE
To the Most Wors/Jipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
The Investment Committee has the responsibility of reP.ortin_g annually to
Grand Lodge on the condition of the various funds of Grand Lodge and those
of its entities.
During the Y.ear quarterly meetings are held bY. the Committee with its investment counselors. At eacn meeting an indepenClent analY!:ical firm reviews
the performance of the P.rimary funds as COf!lpared with similar funds, i.e., endowment, non-profit anCI trust funds, in the United States.
The primary concern of the Committee is the P.reservation of the principal
of the vanous fu!lds together wi~ the highest rate of retu!n commensurate with
safety and good investment practice. Three funds.,. ~asomc Homes Endowment
Fund, Masonic Homes General Fund and the ttugo M. Lorber Union City
Home Fund constitute% percent of the total investments.
Among other funds supcrvi.sed qy the Cof!lmittee ar.e the General F:und 9f
Grand Lodge, tbe funds o Cahforn1a Masonic Memorial Temple, Califorrua
Masonic Foundation and Amaranth, Pooled Income and thirteen restricted-use
funds of the Masonic Homes.
The market value of the total portfolio on June 30, 1987 was $211026000
compared to $188,548p00 a Y.ear earlier;., an increase of 11.9 percent. The 19861987 cash yield from tne total invested 1unds was 6.2 percenl.
Fixed income securities including government and corporate bonds composed 52 percent of the total portfolio. The remainder consisted of common
stocks and cash equivalents.
The Pooled Income Fund is of particular importance to the Masonic
Homes. On June 30, 1987, the Fund had a market va,ue of $3,002,000. The ca~h
yield was 8.6 percent. The Pooled Income Fund &!ves Masons and others m
California and Hawaii the opportunity to create a lifetime income for themselves and for one-time desig_nafed beneficiaries. Certain tax advantages ma~ acalcrue to the contributor. Eventually, the Masonic Homes becomes the lin
beneficiary.
The rewarding accumulation of assets in the various funds of Grand Lodge
has been the resurt of the efforts of Masons and their friends. The operatiocedns
of the Masonic Homes at Union City and Covina are almost entirely fman

The Committee's success achieved this year can be credited to the skillfuJ
and bard work of its co-chairman, Theodore L. Picco\ Robin Mansfield and
frank B. Fiedler. Everett Houser, as Chairman, maintamed general oversight.
Nine day-long workshops were completed in California, five in the South
and four in the NOrth. All were well attended. Co-chairman Fiedler arrang,ed
for wprkshops on the P.rincipal islands in Hawaii, one workshop coinciding with
the vtSlt of the Grand Master.
Regardl~ss of where held, the Committee's efforts met with enthusiastic
response. Written reports on each workshop were made to the Executive Commitlee. A determination was manifest on the part of those attending to raise the
quality of Lodge meetings.

During the last year, a number of "mini workshoQs" were held _presentin_g

in condensed form the highlights of full day sessions. They were well receiveO.

The Inspec~ors and Assistant Grand Lecturers were supportive of the effort. The reduction in travel expense for the "faculty" makes if possible to hold
workshops in the outlying reaches of the Jurisdiction.
Thanks are due the many dedicated Masons who served as the faculty to
the Gran~ Master for his encouragement and to the Grand Secretary for bis
cooperation.

It is recommended that the workshops be continued substantially as this

)'CU, and that the mini workshop program be expanded.

Respectfully submitted,

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON
MASONIC SERVICE BUREAUS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. &A.M. of California:
The Committee on Masonic Service Bureaus is pleased to submit its An·
nual Report on the operations and conditions of the seventeen Masonic Service
Bureaus for the year ending 30 June 1987. The Committee is in its 60th year.
Rigl!t Worshipful Leo B. Mark, Deputy Grand Master, was apP.ointed
liaison officer to tl1e Committee and we appreciate his support and assistance
during the year.
This Committee is well aware of its responsibility in overseeing and directi!Jg the operation of the various Bureaus m a uniform manner. The Service
Bureaus assist sojourners their widows and orphans; ov.erate blood banks; arrange and conduct funerais for deceased Masons; make investigatio ns; assist in
processing applicatic.ms fo.r the two Masonic Homes; visit the sick and promote
fraternal relations "With so1ourners.
NEW COMMITTEE MEMBER
We welcome Worshipful Rodger J. Page, a member of Mosaic Lodge No.
218. B~other Page repla~es WorshiP.ful Ray.Rookard who retired from the
Comnuttee after performmg outstanchng serVlce .
EXECUTIVE SECRETARIES
We were saddened by the passing of WorshiPful Lloyd V. Smith, Executive
Secretary of the Los Angeles Bureau. Brother Smith served that Bureau for a
number of years and his many friends will miss his presence. Brother Arthur H.
Rumsey has been selected tiy the Los Angeles Bureau as Brother Smith's replacement and we greet him and wish him well.
We welcome Brother Gene Capps as the Executive Secretary of the
Masonic Service Bureau of San Jose.
MEETINGS
The Committee lield four meetings during the year. One, which was held
durin_g the first two days of Grand Lodge Week 13 and 14 O ctober,_perrnitted
memt>ers of the vario-µs Bureaus and LOdge offic~rs to conta~t the Committee
and to receive help with the many problems applicable to their areas.
A regional meeting was held in Oakland on February 21, 1987 with 38 members and guests of the bureaus from Northern California in attendance.
A regional meeting was held in Los Angeles on April 25, 1987 with 32 members and guests from Southern California aftending. Chairman Ivie was pleased
to introduce Worshipful Delmer W. May, former cbairman and current advisor
to pie Committee. We were again pleased to have Very Worshipful Robert A.
Klinger, Grand Secretary, as our guest speaker. Prior to adjournment a certifi~ o1 appreciation was presented to Worshipful Lloyd V. Smith, Executive
~etary of the Los Angeles Bureau for his years of outstanding sevice to that

burcau.

On Wednesday, June 10, 1987, the Committee met in Pasadena to review
~-PJ:~posed budgets of the seventeen Masonic Service Bureas in California.
• uc; '-Vmmittee afso reviewed its own budget for the Masonic year 1987-1988.

The Pasadena Scottish Rite graciously provided the facilities fo r our meeting.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

REPORT OF COMMITIEE ON
OLD MASONIC HALLAT LOS ANGELES

The Committee is aQPreciative of the co-o_peration extended by Grand
[..odge and friends of the Temple which has resulted in a banner year.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. &: A.M. of Califomia:
During 1987 the "Old Masonic Hall in Los Angeles" observed its 25th year
of re-~edication by Grand Lodge and enjoyed a year of growth, improvement
and high hopes for the future.
It was in Auzµst 1962, that Grand Lodge, under the direction ofM. W. Guy
B. M~ Grand Master, conducted an all-cfay celebration at the historic Temple
site, 410-l/2 North Main Street, in the northern area of downtown Los Angeles.
The Tem_ple was constructed in 1858. It was the fourth two-story buildin.e
to be built in Los Angeles. From 1858 to 1868 Los Angeles Lodge No. 42 me'(
here. Afterwards, the old Temple remained idle for many years, and like other
pioneer buildings in the Plaza,.i, deteriorated. In 1958, the building was purchased
by the California State Park Lommission and made a part of the Pueblo de Los
Angeles St~te His~orical Pa.r~. Steps were taken to ~estore this early Masonic
Temple to its ongmal condition. After years of dedicated work by many persons, the task has now been completed.
The Old Masonic Hall is still used for Masonic activities. Plaza de Los Angeles Lodge No. 814 meets on Thursday. Other Lodges and concerned Bodies
may rent the Temple facilities. It is open to the public as a Masonic museum on
Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday ancfFriday from 10:00 A.M. to 3:00 P.M.
Highlights of tlze Masonic year:
(1). For the first time, the church organ, donated to the Temple about 75
years ago, was disassembled and overnauJed by an organ professional. Two
fulJ five-octave sets and special beUows were overhauled and cleaned. It
now has a .P.henomenal tone. The footpump organ is used at aU degree
meetings held at the Temple, and is one of its most treasured possessions.
(2). All of the electric switches and meters were replaced with up-to-date
mOdels.
(3). Nearlx two doze.n cane back chairs, donated to the Temple in 1940,
were rebuilt by a cabmet maker.
(4). The Committee is working on a P.roject to accrue hridge tables and
chairs which can be utilized on an aojoming patio for refreshment and
socializing following a degree or special meetmg.
(5) . Nearly 80 Blue Lodges in the Fifth Masonic Division will be canvassed
during the coming year as to whether they wish to display any historic
Masonic artifacts, mementos, regalia~jewelry or historical records in the
enlarged Temple museum. Over 1:>00 visitors, many from European
countries> paid a call to the Hall this year. During school session, classes of
students 1rom elementary and junior high schools frequently stop at the
Museum after they toured the old Plaza area where the Temple is located.
(6) . Rental of the Temple facilities reached a new high this year as nine
LOdges and three Masonic youth organizations conducfed degrees and special meetings. Masonic LOdges pax $45.00 rental fee per night. Youth
grouJ?s are Charged $25.00 for Saturoay morning dates. Lodges aesiring to
rent the Hall should contact Brother Oliver Celaxa, custodian at (213) 6264933 during museum hours, or at his home at night, (818) 912-0444.

Respectfully submitted,
Morris C. Guss, Chainnan

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A .M. of Califomio:
The Public Schools Committee got off to a slow and shaky start at its meeting during, the 1986 Annual Communication. Many of the usual preparations
anCI plannmg for the 1987 observance of Public Schools Week liad not been
made. In particular, none of the necessary artwork and printing had been done·
therefore, it was not possible to distribute the samples of our 1987 materials at
Grand LOdge. With the appointment of a new Chairman and the redoubled efforts of the other Comm1tfeemen, we quickly arr an. ged for our 1987 logg and
poster as well as the other materials to oe made avaifable to the Lodges.!hese
materials were mailed in early December ap.Qroximately two monthsl.ater than
previous practice. Durin,g thiS year of many difficulties, we were aided and counselled bylhe Grand Lodge officers and tlie Grand Lodge office staff. This support has been sincerely appreciated.

The Committee attempts to get its message across by personally contacting each Lodge. Unfortunately, this is possibre only where we have Committeemen in appropriate locations. Even with our allowance of thirty members
we are unable to e:over the entire Jurisdiction .adeguately. In some divisions, i.e'.
VI"'°we have sufficient numbers to meet with most Lodges through their District
Omcers Meetings with the co-operation of the Inspectors. Jn others, i.e. IV
there is but one member to cover all of the Lod,ges between Stockton and
Bakersfield. We have develo~ the outline of a plan, which has obtained the
approval of.t~e Deputy Grand_Master, to develop and train a e<!dre of intercsfed and wdhng Brethren as "Temporary" Committeemen who will assist particularly in the more remote .areas of the Jurisdiction, in making a personal
appeal to Lodges that otherw1se would not have such contact.
Our Committee was not scheduled to make presentations at the 1987
Masonic Leadership Workshops, again due to our lack of planning referred to
above. However, we were _given the opportunity to have a table at nearly each
Workshoj). Also another Committee gave up its presentation time at the Fresno, San Jose Oakland, and Sacramento Workshops, and the Public Schools
Committee ;\adly accepted the opP.ortuniry to fill Chis void. We are appreciali\:e that the feadyrship of the Masonic Leadership Committee offered our Comnuttee presentation time at the 1988 Workshops, and we have accepted.
At the recommendation of the Grand Master, the Public Schools Committee and the Constitution Observance Committee have undertaken the honoring of 99 California eJementary and high school students who were winners of
essay contests regardmg the B1centenmal Observance of the U.S. Constitution.
We have arran_gea for each of these winners to receive a special C.ertificate of
Award.signed py Grand Master Levitt. In addition, the top thirteen winners are
to receive a $100 Savings Bond. Local Lodges have co-operated in making these
presentations at their Constitutional Observances in September.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON TAXATION
To tile Most Worshipful Gra11d Lodge F. & A.M. of California:
This Committee _giv~s advice on lax matters when asked for by the Grand
Lodge, subordinate Lodges, and other organizations under this Jurisdiction
purmg the past Masonic Year, our assistance has been .requested on matters
of income, property, sales and employment taxes. This Annual Report to the
Grand Lodge is a part of the work of this Committee.
The Committee attempts to review the unceasing changes in law, court
decisions, and rulings of Governmental authorities that affect our Fraternity,
and make any recommendations or give any information thought proper.
New ~odel Ar.t ides and Bylaws ~ere promulgal!!d by_the Temple P.roperties Committee durmg the past Masomc Year. As vanous T emple Assoc1at1ons
asked for assistance from th e Committee in adopting Articles consistent with
the new Mo.de! ~rtjcles, the. wor~ l9ad of the Commillee was greatly increased.
No change ID this situation 1s ant1c1pated.
More memhcrs of the Committee are needed. If the Committee did not
work as friends a nd Brother Masons, the greatest difficulties would already have
occurred.
.E ach year, one member of the Committee P.repares a Calendar of Forms
and Returns due bY. subordinate organizations aunng the year to the various
Governmental entities. This1 he submits lo the Grand Secretary, who sends a
copy to the Secretary of eacn
subordinate organization.
Many TemRle Associations have been assisted with their problems. Many
more remain to be helped. We stand ready to serve as best we can.

as to matters of Masonic Taxation, it is the duty olour Committee to render
such advice. The same is true of Masonic component organizations.

ranking Warden, or in the absence of the Master and Wardens, the duly elected
representative in accordanc e with Section 1148, California Masomc Code.

by the Grand Secretary as having been delinquent in the transmission of certificates of the election and installalion of officers of their respective Lodges. Past

1150, California Masonic Code. In accordanc e with Section 1148a, California
Masonic Code when a Master and Warden from the same Lodge are present
at an Annual Communication, and one of said officers serves on a Grand Lodge
Committee entitled to travel and expense reimbursement, be shall be reimbursed under Section 1150, Califorma Masonic Code. The other officer shall
receive reimbursement under Section 1148, California Masonic Code, as the officer representing his Lodge on the floor of Grand Lodge.

I learned a lot from Roland. He impressed UJJ<?n me the fact that there are

You are friends, and as Roland Bach would say, and his son did say

such place as far away." I will relive this year with my friends many times.
The other thing that I want to im pressJou with, before I really start, is that
Masons are not common people. You, an our Fraternity, are somethillg special anq, to be effective, you must, without pretension, accept that fact. You are
somethmg special. More about that later.
